extraction.body: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". But while Alice Huang is said to have stepped down from her role as Megaspeed director near the end of 2023, there were suspicions that she was still heavily involved in the firm's operations, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS C4ADS said that Huang was still "practically in control" of Megaspeed even after she had handed over the reins of the firm. Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies. Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify. "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme. Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded. The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated to lead Nvidia is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing. The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside the company. On Friday, Bessent had blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process". The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate". China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology. In President Donald Trump’s shadow, oppositional media on the left has seen a period of extraordinary growth. An Australian lawmaker said she was "full of gratitude" on Monday as she was discharged from hospital following an alleged attack in October that resulted in her losing both legs. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said the 65-year-old had been discharged four weeks after she was airlifted in for emergency treatment. Monday's papers lead on a potential rethink of age of consent laws to prevent adults having relationships with 16- and 17-year-olds. Miguel Parra Hernandez was hit by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Mario Alberto Morales in Houston on Oct. 10. Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa denied Sunday that the United States has a military base in his country, after an AFP investigation documented an unusual deployment of US aircraft at a facility there.Noboa said Sunday that US military personnel were there solely for "temporary activities" as part of cooperation between the two countries. Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology. CHISINAU, Nov 15 (Reuters) - A former presidential candidate led the vote on Sunday to replace the jailed leader of Moldova's restive, pro-Russian Gagauzia region ‌and will face a Socialist Party candidate in a November 29 runoff, results ‌showed. Eight candidates vied for the position of bashkan, or leader, of Gagauzia, a region in Moldova's south inhabited mainly ​by Turkic-speaking Orthodox Christians who generally favour close ties with Russia. President Donald Trump will meet jointly this week with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the White House said Friday, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries. Estonia said Sunday it would close its border with Russia after stopping what it said was an attempted arson attack by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory."Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna posted on X, citing "clear evidence" that the GRU had ordered the attack. extraction.body: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded. Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat. "In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday. Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China . Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal. The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department. By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement. Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers." And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress. The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage. Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China." Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks. Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public. "We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving. If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him. Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler. Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair. "From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said. The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers. "He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here." The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers. Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way. Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill. "It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation. Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset. Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair. Huang admitted earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company. It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors. But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member. It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound". There was no mention of the accusations of adultery. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO . It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work. Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI. She had previously been photographed with him on several occasions. The tech giant's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected". Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him. She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with US President Donald Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported . She was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, which the firm said had been investigated and debunked. However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singaporean government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless". Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Huang's resignation hits investors large and small. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. The revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.
Huang admitted earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children.
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.
It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors.
But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member.
It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound".
There was no mention of the accusations of adultery.
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO .
It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis.
One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work.
Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced.

And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI.
She had previously been photographed with him on several occasions.

The tech giant's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected".
Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him.
She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with US President Donald Trump.
At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.
US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported .
She was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023.
Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, which the firm said had been investigated and debunked.
However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singaporean government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips.
It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing.
When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.
China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless".
Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Huang's resignation hits investors large and small.
Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.
Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.
The revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China .

extraction.body: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here . Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned. But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all. Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about. But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive. So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out. Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago. And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly. But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more. Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind. I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America. I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him. Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang. Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair. Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups. People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions. Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this? Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie. Where was Nvidia’s security team? extraction.body: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded. Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat. "In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday. Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China . Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal. The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department. By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement. Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers." And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress. The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage. Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China." Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress. But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.

Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.

"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.

Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China .

Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.

Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls

Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.

passages: "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.
When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.
But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member.
Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him.
Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Huang's resignation hits investors large and small.
After news broke out about the first affair, Nvidia launched an independent investigation and hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.
Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced.
The revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China .

extraction.body: One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive. Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset. Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair. Huang admitted earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company. It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors. But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member. It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound". There was no mention of the accusations of adultery. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO . It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work. Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI. She had previously been photographed with him on several occasions. The tech giant's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected". Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him. She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with US President Donald Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported . She was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, which the firm said had been investigated and debunked. However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singaporean government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless". Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Huang's resignation hits investors large and small. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. The revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . After news broke out about the first affair, Nvidia launched an independent investigation and hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

extraction.body: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here . Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned. But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all. Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about. But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive. So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out. Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago. And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly. But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more. Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind. I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America. I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him. Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang. Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair. Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”

extraction.body: Members of Congress are calling on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign, and momentum is building to subpoena the executive, whose company is a leader in advanced artificial intelligence chips. Senate banking committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., doubled down Wednesday on his call for Huang to resign, and a key Democratic House oversight panel member and House Republican piled on. "As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign," Cramer told CNBC, in response to revelations that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy as the chipmaker he co-founded was given permission from the U.S. government to sell its technology to China. Huang, who leads a company that's been a chief beneficiary of the artificial intelligence boom, on Sunday admitted to having an affair with a woman whom news outlets have reported U.S. intelligence concluded was a Chinese spy . The revelation is sending shockwaves through Washington, with lawmakers now fearing that U.S. AI dominance could be at risk. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer said, referring to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." Cramer's comments come on the deadline set by a trio of House lawmakers who requested Huang to testify before their committees on Nov. 18. GOP Reps. Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; John Moolenaar, chair of the Permanent Select Committee on China; and Rick Crawford, who leads the House intelligence panel, called for Huang to appear in a Nov. 4 letter . Congress members in the majority party also have subpoena power, should they choose to use it. Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Wednesday afternoon that they had not yet heard from Huang and that they were giving him until the end of the day to respond. Asked whether the committees were considering subpoenaing Huang if he doesn't agree to appear, Mast said "yes." Moolenaar, when asked the same question, said "all three committees have subpoena power, and I know all three committees have a very serious interest in getting to the bottom of this and having transparency around this." "We are going to continue to pursue this," Moolenaar said. The lawmakers are far from alone in their criticism, concern and outright shock over the affair. And the scrutiny is only expected to intensify with Democrats poised to take over both chambers of Congress in January. Huang has been close with President Donald Trump during the president's second term, traveling on Air Force One to China in May. "Jensen Huang should resign from Nvidia," Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee, told CNBC. Subramanyam is the top Democrat on the panel's Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs. "I didn't agree with his sentiment that there's no downside to exporting chips to China," he said. "But I never thought that he might be having an affair with a Chinese spy who was helping smuggle chips into China at an alarming rate." Rep. Don Bacon , R-Neb., who is retiring from Congress after sometimes bucking Trump, also said the CEO should step down. "From the little I know, yes." Bacon told CNBC in response to whether Huang should resign. "I mean, he allowed himself to get compromised by the Chinese government. Not good." Huang was notably opposed to strict export controls on AI chips to China, which ruffled feathers with China hawks on Capitol Hill. Democrats are widely expected to launch myriad investigations into the White House and industry when they assume control of both chambers of Congress in January. Nvidia is now likely to be at the center of those probes. "There's two parts to this investigation that [need] to happen somewhere immediately," Subramanyam said. "One is what was going on with Nvidia and China, and two is why the administration did nothing about it even though they appeared to have known, and what the administration knew, and what influence the money from Nvidia and Jensen Huang had on this administration, essentially staying silent." Rep. Jay Obernolte , R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, said Tuesday he hopes that the Huang scandal can avoid becoming a distraction in talks about imposing export controls on advanced AI chips. The situation may give Congress additional ammunition as it tries to pass a suite of bills in this year's National Defense Authorization Act to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips. Congress has still not passed the annual defense bill, which is a top priority for lawmakers in the lame-duck session. Those bills include the AI Overwatch Act , the MATCH Act and the Chip Security Act — all of which are aimed at preventing U.S. chip technology from falling into adversarial hands. Sens. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., in a statement following the revelation of Huang's affair, urged their colleagues to include the AI Overwatch Act. Warren, the incoming Senate banking committee chair, sponsored the bill in the Senate with Banks. "Huang's confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related," the senators said. "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips." And Subramanyam warned that what Nvidia does now — and whether Huang remains atop the company — could affect its relationship with Washington and whether lawmakers crack down. "If Nvidia finds out that he knew about what was going on and does nothing about it, then Nvidia is making a choice and us as regulators and as watchdogs need to defend the American people," he said. passages: NEW YORK, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Congress is more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China's access to AI chips in light of news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected ‌Chinese intelligence agent, lawmakers and advocates said.
Three chip-related measures are slated for possible inclusion in the annual defense authorization ‌bill for fiscal year 2027, which began in October.

"The hurdle these bills ‌need to clear is getting the White House onboard," said ​Chris MacKenzie, a spokesman for Americans ​for Responsible Innovation, a Washington nonprofit organization that favors the measures.
In March, the senators had urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses to China and conduct a full security review.
They added: "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips."
Until the US Department of Justice brought indictments tied to chip smuggling last year, Huang and Nvidia had argued there was no such smuggling.
The ⁠company said it complied with export laws.
Nvidia is considered the biggest opponent of both the Chip Security and AI Overwatch ‌acts, according to one former congressional staffer ⁠who had direct contact with the company over several months.
"Congress has the tools to prevent powerful AI chips from getting in the wrong hands and posing a ‌national security risk," Foster posted on X on Monday, in response to ​news of Huang's affair.

The Information Technology Industry ‌Council, whose members include Nvidia, among other groups, has opposed the measures, arguing they could undermine US competitiveness and ​complicate export control policy.
A spokeswoman for the council declined comment on the current Nvidia situation.

NEW YORK, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Congress is more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China's access to AI chips in light of news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected ‌Chinese intelligence agent, lawmakers and advocates said. Three chip-related measures are slated for possible inclusion in the annual defense authorization ‌bill for fiscal year 2027, which began in October. Huang's affair, and his close relationship with President Donald Trump, has added new urgency to concerns about China's ​access to advanced chips that could undermine US national security. The measures are the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over advanced chip exports, the Chip Security Act, which would require businesses to track their chips to combat smuggling, and the Match Act, which would push US allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment to China. Nvidia is considered the biggest opponent of both the Chip Security and AI Overwatch ‌acts, according to one former congressional staffer ⁠who had direct contact with the company over several months. Until the US Department of Justice brought indictments tied to chip smuggling last year, Huang and Nvidia had argued there was no such smuggling. The ⁠company said it complied with export laws. US HOUSE Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday (Nov 12) there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government.

Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China’s surging AI development. And senior White House officials were discussing whether Commerce ​Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation said, as the desire to take action rose across Washington.

A growing number of lawmakers have criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.”

The Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.
The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.

Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent ​Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company’s chips remotely.

Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defence authorisation Bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically ​attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four Bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require ​companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.

The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centres to access Nvidia chips.

Huang’s resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation.
“Congress can still subpoena him and Nvidia should conduct an independent investigation to determine whether the problems extend beyond Huang,” Cheung said.

Cheung said Huang’s departure could weaken Nvidia’s influence in Washington and create additional momentum for legislation that tightens restrictions on advanced chip exports. He said Nvidia’s new leadership could also reconsider the company’s China strategy as it seeks to rebuild trust with US policymakers.

Jensen Huang is separately expected to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, which falls on Nov 26. House Foreign Affairs chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke with Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for his testimony.
Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with Alice Huang. REUTERS

extraction.body: Members of Congress are calling on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign, and momentum is building to subpoena the executive, whose company is a leader in advanced artificial intelligence chips. Senate banking committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., doubled down Wednesday on his call for Huang to resign, and a key Democratic House oversight panel member and House Republican piled on. "As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign," Cramer told CNBC, in response to revelations that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy as the chipmaker he co-founded was given permission from the U.S. government to sell its technology to China. Huang, who leads a company that's been a chief beneficiary of the artificial intelligence boom, on Sunday admitted to having an affair with a woman whom news outlets have reported U.S. intelligence concluded was a Chinese spy . The revelation is sending shockwaves through Washington, with lawmakers now fearing that U.S. AI dominance could be at risk. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer said, referring to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." Cramer's comments come on the deadline set by a trio of House lawmakers who requested Huang to testify before their committees on Nov. 18. GOP Reps. Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; John Moolenaar, chair of the Permanent Select Committee on China; and Rick Crawford, who leads the House intelligence panel, called for Huang to appear in a Nov. 4 letter . Congress members in the majority party also have subpoena power, should they choose to use it. Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Wednesday afternoon that they had not yet heard from Huang and that they were giving him until the end of the day to respond. Asked whether the committees were considering subpoenaing Huang if he doesn't agree to appear, Mast said "yes." Moolenaar, when asked the same question, said "all three committees have subpoena power, and I know all three committees have a very serious interest in getting to the bottom of this and having transparency around this." "We are going to continue to pursue this," Moolenaar said. The lawmakers are far from alone in their criticism, concern and outright shock over the affair. And the scrutiny is only expected to intensify with Democrats poised to take over both chambers of Congress in January. Huang has been close with President Donald Trump during the president's second term, traveling on Air Force One to China in May. "Jensen Huang should resign from Nvidia," Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee, told CNBC. Subramanyam is the top Democrat on the panel's Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs. "I didn't agree with his sentiment that there's no downside to exporting chips to China," he said. "But I never thought that he might be having an affair with a Chinese spy who was helping smuggle chips into China at an alarming rate." Rep. Don Bacon , R-Neb., who is retiring from Congress after sometimes bucking Trump, also said the CEO should step down. "From the little I know, yes." Bacon told CNBC in response to whether Huang should resign. "I mean, he allowed himself to get compromised by the Chinese government. Not good." Huang was notably opposed to strict export controls on AI chips to China, which ruffled feathers with China hawks on Capitol Hill. Democrats are widely expected to launch myriad investigations into the White House and industry when they assume control of both chambers of Congress in January. Nvidia is now likely to be at the center of those probes. "There's two parts to this investigation that [need] to happen somewhere immediately," Subramanyam said. "One is what was going on with Nvidia and China, and two is why the administration did nothing about it even though they appeared to have known, and what the administration knew, and what influence the money from Nvidia and Jensen Huang had on this administration, essentially staying silent." Rep. Jay Obernolte , R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, said Tuesday he hopes that the Huang scandal can avoid becoming a distraction in talks about imposing export controls on advanced AI chips. The situation may give Congress additional ammunition as it tries to pass a suite of bills in this year's National Defense Authorization Act to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips. Congress has still not passed the annual defense bill, which is a top priority for lawmakers in the lame-duck session. Those bills include the AI Overwatch Act , the MATCH Act and the Chip Security Act — all of which are aimed at preventing U.S. chip technology from falling into adversarial hands. Sens. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., in a statement following the revelation of Huang's affair, urged their colleagues to include the AI Overwatch Act. Warren, the incoming Senate banking committee chair, sponsored the bill in the Senate with Banks. "Huang's confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related," the senators said. "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips." And Subramanyam warned that what Nvidia does now — and whether Huang remains atop the company — could affect its relationship with Washington and whether lawmakers crack down. "If Nvidia finds out that he knew about what was going on and does nothing about it, then Nvidia is making a choice and us as regulators and as watchdogs need to defend the American people," he said. NEW YORK, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Congress is more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China's access to AI chips in light of news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected ‌Chinese intelligence agent, lawmakers and advocates said.

Three chip-related measures are slated for possible inclusion in the annual defense authorization ‌bill for fiscal year 2027, which began in October. Huang's affair, and his close relationship with President Donald Trump, has added new urgency to concerns about China's ​access to advanced chips that could undermine US national security.

The measures are the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over advanced chip exports, the Chip Security Act, which would require businesses to track their chips to combat smuggling, and the Match Act, which would push US allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment to China.
Nvidia is considered the biggest opponent of both the Chip Security and AI Overwatch ‌acts, according to one former congressional staffer ⁠who had direct contact with the company over several months.
Until the US Department of Justice brought indictments tied to chip smuggling last year, Huang and Nvidia had argued there was no such smuggling. The ⁠company said it complied with export laws.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all three bills earlier this year. They are now in the Senate National Defense Authorization Act management package.

In a joint statement on Monday, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and her Republican colleague ​Jim ​Banks of Indiana said that "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's confirmation of a relationship ​with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes ‌these national security concerns even more urgent."
They added: "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips."
In March, the senators had urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses to China and conduct a full security review.

Democratic Representative Bill Foster of Illinois echoed the senators' sentiments. "Congress has the tools to prevent powerful AI chips from getting in the wrong hands and posing a ‌national security risk," Foster posted on X on Monday, in response to ​news of Huang's affair.

He said the Chip Security Act he introduced with Republican ​Representative Bill Huizenga of Michigan had passed unanimously out of ​committee in the House. "It's time to get it across the finish line," he said.

"The hurdle these bills ‌need to clear is getting the White House onboard," said ​Chris MacKenzie, a spokesman for Americans ​for Responsible Innovation, a Washington nonprofit organization that favors the measures. "With everything that's surfaced, it would be costly for the White House to back Nvidia in a fight with Congress over restricting Chinese access to chips."
The White House did not ​comment on the measures.

The Information Technology Industry ‌Council, whose members include Nvidia, among other groups, has opposed the measures, arguing they could undermine US competitiveness and ​complicate export control policy. A spokeswoman for the council declined comment on the current Nvidia situation.
(Reporting by Karen ​Freifeld in New York; editing by Chris Sanders and David Gaffen)

US HOUSE Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday (Nov 12) there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government.

Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China’s surging AI development. And senior White House officials were discussing whether Commerce ​Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation said, as the desire to take action rose across Washington.

A growing number of lawmakers have criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.”

The Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.
The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.

Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent ​Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company’s chips remotely.

Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defence authorisation Bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically ​attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four Bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require ​companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.

The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centres to access Nvidia chips.

Huang’s resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation.
“Congress can still subpoena him and Nvidia should conduct an independent investigation to determine whether the problems extend beyond Huang,” Cheung said.

Cheung said Huang’s departure could weaken Nvidia’s influence in Washington and create additional momentum for legislation that tightens restrictions on advanced chip exports. He said Nvidia’s new leadership could also reconsider the company’s China strategy as it seeks to rebuild trust with US policymakers.

Jensen Huang is separately expected to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, which falls on Nov 26.
