extraction.body: Just three days after the high-profile resignation of the founder of the world's most valuable chipmaker, his supporters in Silicon Valley have set up a dedicated war room to pressure the board of directors. However, regaining the seat will not be easy for the billionaire: he does not hold a controlling stake, while the corporation is already scouting for his replacement and bracing for scrutiny from Washington. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday, November 12, following the exposure of extramarital relationships with an alleged Chinese spy and a direct subordinate, is already discussing a plan to return to the company with his confidants. This was reported on Sunday, November 15, by the British newspaper Financial Times. According to an associate of the businessman, Silicon Valley top executives have formed a dedicated "war room" to lobby Nvidia's board of directors for Huang's reinstatement, as well as to try to secure support in the White House. "Everyone who matters in tech outside of the frontier labs loves Jensen," said an interlocutor of the publication, adding that these efforts have the backing of the former CEO himself. Over the weekend, the public campaign for the return of the founder of the $4 trillion corporation gained momentum. An open letter to the board of directors demanding to "Bring Jensen Back" was supported by Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as several Nvidia employees. Back on Friday, major shareholders of the company—Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management head Gavin Baker—published an appeal to the corporate leadership, urging them to keep "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang," given his decades of service and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the business. Despite pressure from billionaires and investors, the push to rehabilitate Huang faces severe legal and political obstacles. Unlike many other tech titan founders, Huang does not hold a controlling stake in Nvidia and therefore cannot veto decisions made by the board of directors. The board itself is currently conducting an independent investigation into the former chief's conduct. Even those in the businessman's camp acknowledge the weakness of his position. "An affair with a subordinate is a firing offense," admitted one member of Huang's support group. Aside from the internal workplace affair with Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell, Huang's primary problem stems from his connection to Alice Huang, head of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which US authorities suspect of espionage and smuggling chips into China. This episode has drawn intense scrutiny toward how Nvidia monitors the sales of its artificial intelligence processors to clients in Asia. On Sunday, November 15, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly called for a "radical refresh" in Nvidia's leadership following the departure of its founder. Meanwhile, the corporation's interim CEO Colette Kress is preparing the company for the release of its quarterly financial report on Tuesday, while the board of directors is already looking for a permanent successor. According to the Financial Times, Nvidia representatives have approached Rene Haas, CEO of the British processor architecture designer Arm Holdings, with an offer to head the corporation, though officially the company states that a formal process to select a new leader has not yet been launched. Representatives of Nvidia and Jensen Huang himself declined to comment on his potential return.

extraction.body: An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email. Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips. It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED. Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.” Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

extraction.body: Just three days after the high-profile resignation of the founder of the world's most valuable chipmaker, his supporters in Silicon Valley have set up a dedicated war room to pressure the board of directors. However, regaining the seat will not be easy for the billionaire: he does not hold a controlling stake, while the corporation is already scouting for his replacement and bracing for scrutiny from Washington. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday, November 12, following the exposure of extramarital relationships with an alleged Chinese spy and a direct subordinate, is already discussing a plan to return to the company with his confidants. This was reported on Sunday, November 15, by the British newspaper Financial Times. According to an associate of the businessman, Silicon Valley top executives have formed a dedicated "war room" to lobby Nvidia's board of directors for Huang's reinstatement, as well as to try to secure support in the White House. "Everyone who matters in tech outside of the frontier labs loves Jensen," said an interlocutor of the publication, adding that these efforts have the backing of the former CEO himself. Over the weekend, the public campaign for the return of the founder of the $4 trillion corporation gained momentum. An open letter to the board of directors demanding to "Bring Jensen Back" was supported by Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as several Nvidia employees. Back on Friday, major shareholders of the company—Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management head Gavin Baker—published an appeal to the corporate leadership, urging them to keep "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang," given his decades of service and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the business. Despite pressure from billionaires and investors, the push to rehabilitate Huang faces severe legal and political obstacles. Unlike many other tech titan founders, Huang does not hold a controlling stake in Nvidia and therefore cannot veto decisions made by the board of directors. The board itself is currently conducting an independent investigation into the former chief's conduct. Even those in the businessman's camp acknowledge the weakness of his position. "An affair with a subordinate is a firing offense," admitted one member of Huang's support group. Aside from the internal workplace affair with Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell, Huang's primary problem stems from his connection to Alice Huang, head of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which US authorities suspect of espionage and smuggling chips into China. This episode has drawn intense scrutiny toward how Nvidia monitors the sales of its artificial intelligence processors to clients in Asia. On Sunday, November 15, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly called for a "radical refresh" in Nvidia's leadership following the departure of its founder. Meanwhile, the corporation's interim CEO Colette Kress is preparing the company for the release of its quarterly financial report on Tuesday, while the board of directors is already looking for a permanent successor. According to the Financial Times, Nvidia representatives have approached Rene Haas, CEO of the British processor architecture designer Arm Holdings, with an offer to head the corporation, though officially the company states that a formal process to select a new leader has not yet been launched. Representatives of Nvidia and Jensen Huang himself declined to comment on his potential return.

extraction.body: Apple’s smart glasses are among the worst-kept secrets in the tech world. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the company’s first model, which will lack augmented reality features, will be announced at June’s WWDC next year. They likely won’t ship right away, however, with Gurman saying only that “glasses shipments would begin before the end of the year.” Key to their success will be the newly revamped Siri AI, which is adding fine-grained control over apps. By adding those features now and letting developers add support on the iPhone first, it’s hoping that its smart glasses will be able to hit the ground running. They also have a MagSafe-like charger Gurman describes as “flat, rectangular” and “roughly the size of a Tic Tac,” which can be used even while still wearing the glasses. In addition to Apple putting an emphasis on style, privacy, and audio quality, the company is also hoping that Wi-Fi connectivity will grant them a certain amount of freedom, despite relying on an iPhone to actually execute many tasks: > The glasses have Wi-Fi, allowing certain functions outside of third-party apps to continue working when the iPhone isn’t nearby. Users could theoretically keep listening to audio over Wi-Fi after walking away from their phones, for instance, though the eyewear won’t operate as a fully independent device. Apple is also emphasizing the sound quality, which employees have said is industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music playback and FaceTime audio communication.

passages: Apple’s first smart glasses will rely on Siri to control apps on a paired iPhone, according to a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.
The glasses will reportedly need a recent iPhone, and current plans include no Android support.
As of November 16, Apple has not commented on the report.
For Android owners, the iPhone requirement is the key detail.
That leaves Android users with options like Meta’s Ray-Ban line and Google and Samsung’s Android XR glasses, which start at $395 .
Siri’s app-action controls arrived in the first iOS 27.3 beta, per the report.
It fits with earlier reporting that Siri could become an AI agent that acts inside apps for you.
Plans can change before a 2027 launch, so this isn’t a final word on Android compatibility.
Apple is also said to be experimenting with extra privacy features.
Recording indicators matter on camera glasses, as Ray-Ban Meta owners’ reports of unprompted recordings showed earlier.
They stay on the iPhone, and developers would not build separate glasses apps.

extraction.body: Apple’s first smart glasses will rely on Siri to control apps on a paired iPhone, according to a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The glasses will reportedly need a recent iPhone, and current plans include no Android support. As of November 16, Apple has not commented on the report. The glasses, code-named N50, are reportedly due to be unveiled at WWDC in June 2027. Shipments would begin before the end of that year. Gurman cautions that the software and AI work is running late, so that timeline could slip. The first model reportedly has no AR display. Instead, Siri would use the built-in cameras to answer questions about what you’re looking at. The report’s examples include identifying a building and suggesting meals from what’s in your fridge. Siri could also give directions and translate signs or conversations. Apps would not run on the glasses themselves. They stay on the iPhone, and developers would not build separate glasses apps. Instead, they would let Siri trigger specific features inside their existing iPhone apps. Think booking a ride, reserving a table, ordering coffee or buying movie tickets. Some of that groundwork is already in place. Siri’s app-action controls arrived in the first iOS 27.3 beta, per the report. Apple’s own apps get support in December, and third-party apps follow in 2027. It fits with earlier reporting that Siri could become an AI agent that acts inside apps for you. Beyond Siri, the glasses would handle calls, messages, notifications, calendars and reminders. Music playback and smart-home controls are on the list too. Employees reportedly rate the audio among the best in the industry. Gurman describes the current prototype as slightly thinner than Meta’s second-generation Ray-Ban glasses. Oval camera openings sit flush in the frame. A light on the front shows when the glasses are in use or charging. Apple is also said to be experimenting with extra privacy features. Recording indicators matter on camera glasses, as Ray-Ban Meta owners’ reports of unprompted recordings showed earlier. Charging uses a flat, three-pin magnetic connector near the end of the left temple arm. The report puts it at roughly the size of a Tic Tac. It’s not yet clear whether that design will make it to the final product. Inside, the prototypes run a reduced version of visionOS 28. The chip is reportedly derived from older Apple Watch processors. Wi-Fi keeps some functions, such as audio, working without an iPhone nearby. Even so, the glasses are not meant to be a standalone device. For Android owners, the iPhone requirement is the key detail. Under current plans, Apple’s glasses won’t pair with Android phones. That leaves Android users with options like Meta’s Ray-Ban line and Google and Samsung’s Android XR glasses, which start at $395 . Plans can change before a 2027 launch, so this isn’t a final word on Android compatibility. The report doesn’t mention pricing. Gurman adds that Apple’s camera-equipped AirPods are still planned for late 2027. Source: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, via MacRumors , The Verge

extraction.body: As soon as next year, Apple will be debuting its first pair of AI-powered smart glasses. They’ll integrate Visual Intelligence and bring Siri to the real world. Here’s what we’re expecting. First and foremost, these glasses are AI glasses, not AR glasses. That means they’ll primarily be voice and camera-based, as they won’t have any displays. The cameras will allow Siri to look at your real world environment and answer questions, provide context, and translate signage. Another feature that we’ll likely see on these glasses is the ability for you to ask Siri to save an image of something and remind you later, as we first saw in the macOS 26.7 leak . They’ll also offer speakers for music and audio playback, so you can think of them as open-ear headphones. On the other hand, though – they might not allow for the glasses to take photos and videos normally, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses have become a massive privacy concern lately, and Apple may want to avoid that. Unlike Meta, Apple isn’t partnering with an existing eyewear-maker to design these glasses. According to Bloomberg , the company is instead designing them in house, with a number of different styles in the works: They’re supposedly going to be made of acetate, a more durable and higher-end alternative to plastic. Apple will also offer them in a few finishes, including black, ocean blue, and light brown. In a future iteration of the product, Apple is reportedly considering positioning the product as a health device. This could mean they’ll integrate heart-rate monitors (similar to AirPods Pro 3 ), and it could mean there’ll be additional software features (like Workout Buddy from Apple Watch) to make it more helpful. Beyond that, it’s unclear how Apple will make these useful for health – just don’t expect it in the first iteration. Just like Apple Vision Pro; it’s a niche product. People don’t wear glasses unless they’re sunglasses or prescribed. People are way more comfortable interacting with a device they can hold in their hands. Another device going to languish away on the table at your nearest Apple Store. Spatial Computing is not the next big thing for the masses. People still want the same thing they’ve always wanted. sources.title: Apple’s First Smart Glasses Will Be iPhone-Only, Gurman Reports - AndroidPure
passages: Apple’s first smart glasses will rely on Siri to control apps on a paired iPhone, according to a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.
The glasses will reportedly need a recent iPhone, and current plans include no Android support.
As of November 16, Apple has not commented on the report.
For Android owners, the iPhone requirement is the key detail.
That leaves Android users with options like Meta’s Ray-Ban line and Google and Samsung’s Android XR glasses, which start at $395 .
Siri’s app-action controls arrived in the first iOS 27.3 beta, per the report.
It fits with earlier reporting that Siri could become an AI agent that acts inside apps for you.
Plans can change before a 2027 launch, so this isn’t a final word on Android compatibility.
Apple is also said to be experimenting with extra privacy features.
Recording indicators matter on camera glasses, as Ray-Ban Meta owners’ reports of unprompted recordings showed earlier.
They stay on the iPhone, and developers would not build separate glasses apps.

extraction.body: Apple’s first smart glasses will rely on Siri to control apps on a paired iPhone, according to a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The glasses will reportedly need a recent iPhone, and current plans include no Android support. As of November 16, Apple has not commented on the report. The glasses, code-named N50, are reportedly due to be unveiled at WWDC in June 2027. Shipments would begin before the end of that year. Gurman cautions that the software and AI work is running late, so that timeline could slip. The first model reportedly has no AR display. Instead, Siri would use the built-in cameras to answer questions about what you’re looking at. The report’s examples include identifying a building and suggesting meals from what’s in your fridge. Siri could also give directions and translate signs or conversations. Apps would not run on the glasses themselves. They stay on the iPhone, and developers would not build separate glasses apps. Instead, they would let Siri trigger specific features inside their existing iPhone apps. Think booking a ride, reserving a table, ordering coffee or buying movie tickets. Some of that groundwork is already in place. Siri’s app-action controls arrived in the first iOS 27.3 beta, per the report. Apple’s own apps get support in December, and third-party apps follow in 2027. It fits with earlier reporting that Siri could become an AI agent that acts inside apps for you. Beyond Siri, the glasses would handle calls, messages, notifications, calendars and reminders. Music playback and smart-home controls are on the list too. Employees reportedly rate the audio among the best in the industry. Gurman describes the current prototype as slightly thinner than Meta’s second-generation Ray-Ban glasses. Oval camera openings sit flush in the frame. A light on the front shows when the glasses are in use or charging. Apple is also said to be experimenting with extra privacy features. Recording indicators matter on camera glasses, as Ray-Ban Meta owners’ reports of unprompted recordings showed earlier. Charging uses a flat, three-pin magnetic connector near the end of the left temple arm. The report puts it at roughly the size of a Tic Tac. It’s not yet clear whether that design will make it to the final product. Inside, the prototypes run a reduced version of visionOS 28. The chip is reportedly derived from older Apple Watch processors. Wi-Fi keeps some functions, such as audio, working without an iPhone nearby. Even so, the glasses are not meant to be a standalone device. For Android owners, the iPhone requirement is the key detail. Under current plans, Apple’s glasses won’t pair with Android phones. That leaves Android users with options like Meta’s Ray-Ban line and Google and Samsung’s Android XR glasses, which start at $395 . Plans can change before a 2027 launch, so this isn’t a final word on Android compatibility. The report doesn’t mention pricing. Gurman adds that Apple’s camera-equipped AirPods are still planned for late 2027. Source: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, via MacRumors , The Verge

passages: A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company's recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.
The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders.
Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Nvidia's stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang's departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding .

The petition states that its signers are "concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process" and demands that the board "bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts." It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

A petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has attracted over 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon, with the petition website listing 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders among signers. Elon Musk signed the petition and wrote on X, “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I'm signing it too,” while the petition text says signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process.” Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement, and the board has not publicly identified a new CEO.

The petition also demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts,” and it urges directors to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public. An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation drew more than 1,600 comments, with one anonymous commenter writing, “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss.”

The petition’s open letter to Nvidia’s board argues that the board removed Huang without “meaningful due process” and says signers have “not been shown evidence that the woman at the centre of the controversy was a spy.” The petition also states, “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership,” and it asks for an independent inquiry with a disclosed scope and timeline before a final decision. Huang wrote to employees on Sunday admitting he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse,” after reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

The Times of India reported that Huang’s resignation followed reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report, and it said the board announced his resignation on Thursday morning. Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management Managing Partner Gavin Baker urged Nvidia’s board to pursue a “slow, measured, and deliberate process,” arguing that “There are more questions about recent events than answers.”

Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” and the board said it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets had been compromised.

Nvidia announced on November 12 that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and a member of its board, effective immediately, and it said Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO while the board began a search for a permanent successor.
Harvey C. Jones was appointed the company’s first-ever board chair, and the leadership transition is scheduled to coincide with Nvidia’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on November 17.

The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.
Elon Musk told the Washington Post that he’d signed a petition for Huang’s reinstatement, and the petition campaign website said it was “actively working” to remove fake signatures.
Business Insider stresses fake-signature removal, while The Federal stresses self-reported, unverified signers, shaping credibility differently.

Our editorials offer in-depth analysis curated by the NewsCord team. A petition to reinstate Jensen Huang has over 115,000 signatories including shareholders and employees. Elon Musk signed the petition endorsing Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. Headlines report petitions and endorsements calling for Jensen Huang’s return, with many highlighting prominent supporters. The coverage describes a campaign for reinstatement; it does not indicate that Nvidia has agreed to bring him back. Several headlines name Elon Musk or other investors and technology executives as supporters of a petition or campaign seeking Jensen Huang’s reinstatement. Their reported endorsement does not show that Nvidia’s board has accepted the request. Petitions and employee calls seek Huang’s return Reviewed by Codex validator (AI) · 15 Nov 2026 A petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has attracted over 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon, with the petition website listing 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders among signers. Elon Musk signed the petition and wrote on X, “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I'm signing it too,” while the petition text says signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process.” Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement, and the board has not publicly identified a new CEO. The petition also demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts,” and it urges directors to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public. An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation drew more than 1,600 comments, with one anonymous commenter writing, “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss.” The petition’s open letter to Nvidia’s board argues that the board removed Huang without “meaningful due process” and says signers have “not been shown evidence that the woman at the centre of the controversy was a spy.” The petition also states, “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership,” and it asks for an independent inquiry with a disclosed scope and timeline before a final decision. Huang wrote to employees on Sunday admitting he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse,” after reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The Times of India reported that Huang’s resignation followed reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report, and it said the board announced his resignation on Thursday morning. Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management Managing Partner Gavin Baker urged Nvidia’s board to pursue a “slow, measured, and deliberate process,” arguing that “There are more questions about recent events than answers.” Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” and the board said it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets had been compromised. Consumer health technologies powered by LLMs may at times offer responses that are incomplete or unclear, which is why research is critical to presenting health information to users with greater clarity. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine. “When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Participants retain control over whether to share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses, and Apple has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information. The study app features safety guardrails that are intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed. The latest news and updates, direct from Apple.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding.
Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled.

Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models.
The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple launches research study to explore the use of AI for health

Apple today announced the launch of the Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States, a virtual research study and associated app designed to advance the understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools.

1 By examining what drives user trust, the quality of responses, comprehension, and everyday health actions, the study aims to inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for Apple and the industry.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”
The study brings together medically grounded AI technology developed by OpenEvidence with an Apple-designed research experience.

Consumer health technologies powered by LLMs may at times offer responses that are incomplete or unclear, which is why research is critical to presenting health information to users with greater clarity.
The study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency, and clinical guardrails, and study data will not be used to train AI models.
The latest news and updates, direct from Apple.
Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features.
Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health.
But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding.
Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled.
The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.
The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users.
It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet.
Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models.
The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.
The company announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study on November 15, 2026, in partnership with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform built for healthcare professionals.
For Apple, the study offers something valuable: large-scale, structured feedback on how people engage with health AI before committing to a consumer product.
The study departs from Apple’s earlier health research, which centered on data collected by its devices.
Apple wants to know whether AI health answers are actually any good.
Rather than guess, it is asking up to 200,000 people to grade them.

Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine. “When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. The Apple Health AI Usage Study, conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, will evaluate trust, comprehension, and real-world health AI engagement

Apple today announced the launch of the Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States, a virtual research study and associated app designed to advance the understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools. 1 By examining what drives user trust, the quality of responses, comprehension, and everyday health actions, the study aims to inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for Apple and the industry.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness. “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”

The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine , Journal of the American Medical Association , and Nature . The study brings together medically grounded AI technology developed by OpenEvidence with an Apple-designed research experience. Participants will be able to ask the study app everyday health questions; explore complex medical information communicated with approachable language; and see linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations that ground each response. Participants can also choose to share HealthKit data types — such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results — to explore how personal data integration impacts relevance and understanding. Consumer health technologies powered by LLMs may at times offer responses that are incomplete or unclear, which is why research is critical to presenting health information to users with greater clarity. The study will also explore how health AI can potentially help participants better prepare for clinical visits with their own doctors.

“Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine. “When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Connecting these tools, and rigorously studying what works, is how we’ll get there.”

The study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency, and clinical guardrails, and study data will not be used to train AI models. Participants retain control over whether to share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses, and Apple has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information. The study app features safety guardrails that are intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed.

Since 2019, when Apple first launched its Research app, the company has partnered with medical universities and institutions to run a range of health studies on hearing, heart health and movement, women’s health and, most recently, the Apple Health Study , which covers a wide variety of health areas. To inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for both Apple and the industry and to explore how health AI might help people prepare for doctor’s visits. Key questions the study aims to address include: Do users understand the information provided by health AI? Do they trust it? Is it helpful? This is particularly relevant considering that one in three US adults use AI chatbots for health information. Study data will not be used to train AI models, but it may inform Apple’s feature development. To facilitate the study, Apple is partnering with OpenEvidence, an AI platform designed specifically for doctors. It generates answers using medical information from these partners: The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, National Comprehensive Cancer Network, Nature and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. In the dedicated app, study participants can ask the AI their text-based health questions and then see answers with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations. They can also choose to share their HealthKit data, including sleep, lab results, activity and resting heart rate, for more personalized answers. HealthKit is Apple’s hub for health and fitness data collected on the iPhone and Apple Watch. The Apple Health AI Usage Study is open to 200,000 participants. You must be in the US and age 21 or older to participate. An Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later is also required. Why an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone? According to Apple, the study app requires the processing capabilities of those iPhones, and it uses on-device Apple Foundation Models that are part of Apple Intelligence. These models provide access to any large language model. For example, as part of the study, these models are used to classify question categories. Each participant is asked to participate for up to 12 months. During this time, they can ask questions about general health, specific symptoms, recovery from a procedure and their own uploaded health data, as examples. In addition to a baseline survey, participants will receive monthly surveys and additional surveys specific to preparing for doctor’s visits. Participants will also be prompted to check in with the app. For instance, if you have a paired Apple Watch, you will receive notifications to check in, along with suggested topics to explore. If there is a complete lack of participation, a participant may potentially be removed from the study. Lastly, this info is sent to OpenEvidence, where answers are generated using supporting reference materials. OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours. There is no live monitoring, and study staff won’t contact participants if any questions related to self-harm are asked. It’s also up to the participant whether they share any HealthKit metrics. They will first have to choose to upload their clinical health records to Apple’s Health app, and then separately choose to share those records from the Health app to the new Apple Health AI Study app. The Apple Health AI Study app is now available in the App Store . As of now, there is no set publication date for the study. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

sources.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
passages: China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing.

On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. sources.title: Jensen Huang exit, US scrutiny imperil US$3 billion in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia - The Business Times
passages: [BEIJING] Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s artificial intelligence data centre market, but a Reuters review has identified more than US$3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors.

The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing .
Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation , saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised.
There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.
Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom .
The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.

The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

The company has also excluded China data centre computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty. That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. While Nvidia’s statements address its own ability to compete and sell directly in China, the documents Reuters reviewed show Chinese customers continuing to plan purchases and, in some cases, operating restricted processors. Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement. “Washington must stop focusing solely on who buys the chips on the surface and start examining who ultimately uses the computing power – and for what purpose,” said Cheung. Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls. Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800. coreStoryFacts.text: Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump.

The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.
Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports.
H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.
Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.
Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information.
Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China.
China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing.

On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects.

Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change.

There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.

The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.

passages: China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing.

On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. sources.title: Jensen Huang exit, US scrutiny imperil US$3 billion in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia - The Business Times
passages: [BEIJING] Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s artificial intelligence data centre market, but a Reuters review has identified more than US$3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors.

The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing .
Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation , saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised.
There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34 per cent of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said in 2025 Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95 per cent to zero.
Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global AI boom .
The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations.
It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.

The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

The company has also excluded China data centre computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty. That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. While Nvidia’s statements address its own ability to compete and sell directly in China, the documents Reuters reviewed show Chinese customers continuing to plan purchases and, in some cases, operating restricted processors. Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement. “Washington must stop focusing solely on who buys the chips on the surface and start examining who ultimately uses the computing power – and for what purpose,” said Cheung. Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800. The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday (Nov 12), following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed .
Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors.

These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites – such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before end-2026, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang.
The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

extraction.body: The commerce secretary has been writing new rules that would affect Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of his former firm. Ana Swanson reported from Washington, Aaron Krolik from New York and Paul Mozur from Taiwan. In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers. The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms. The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business. Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A.I. computing power to Chinese firms. The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A.I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia. Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U.S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration. extraction.body: President Donald Trump (left) and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick An investment firm founded by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has close ties to a Southeast Asian AI data center operator capable of supplying cutting-edge artificial intelligence semiconductor technology to China while bypassing U.S. regulations, The New York Times (NYT) reported on the 15th local time. The controversy surrounding Secretary Lutnick, who is at the center of suspicions over delays and suspensions in the Trump administration's export controls on advanced semiconductors to China due to the "Jensen Huang scandal," appears to be expanding into allegations of pursuing private interests. According to the NYT report, Bitdeer, a Singaporean company operating an AI data center named "A201" in southern Malaysia set to open next year, is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, a financial services firm founded by Secretary Lutnick and currently run by his son. Cantor Fitzgerald participated as a designated sales agent when Bitdeer carried out a stock offering worth up to $1 billion this year. In 2024 as well, Cantor Fitzgerald helped arrange a stock offering for Bitdeer valued at up to $250 million. This business structure is both legal and highly profitable. It also allows for circumventing U.S. regulations that ban the sale of cutting-edge AI semiconductors to Chinese companies. The NYT pointed out that beyond this, Cantor Fitzgerald has maintained business relationships with several data center companies in Southeast Asia targeting Chinese clients, which could be affected by regulations currently being prepared by the Commerce Department under Secretary Lutnick. While noting there is no evidence that these investments by Cantor Fitzgerald influenced Secretary Lutnick's decision-making, the NYT highlighted that the relationship between Cantor Fitzgerald and the Southeast Asian data centers "illustrates a potential conflict of interest given the role Secretary Lutnick plays in shaping export-related regulations." The Trump administration has previously engaged in internal debates over the scope of semiconductor sales regulations targeting data centers in Southeast Asia. While hardliners view such data centers as a loophole bypassing export bans to China, Secretary Lutnick has been known to oppose overly restricting U.S. companies like Nvidia from selling semiconductors to Asia. Secretary Lutnick has reportedly delayed or suspended such export restrictions and controls over the past year on multiple occasions, arguing that they could negatively impact Nvidia or U.S.-China trade relations. In particular, sources told the NYT that the Commerce Department has been pushing for a version that significantly scales back the scope of these export restrictions and controls. According to reports, the plans involve applying regulations only to a select few countries—such as Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, South Africa, and Norway—applying them solely to cutting-edge semiconductors shipped going forward, and exempting data centers already built with U.S. technology from regulatory targets. Amid this situation, Secretary Lutnick has found himself cornered following the eruption of a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. U.S. internet media outlet Axios noted, "Secretary Lutnick has become a symbol of the Trump administration's lackluster response to Chinese espionage activities and potential national security threats," adding, "The strongest criticisms are coming from Republican lawmakers, fellow cabinet members, and MAGA, President Trump's core support base." Ultimately, individuals around President Trump and within the Republican Party also want Secretary Lutnick to take responsibility for this crisis. However, President Trump is reportedly maintaining his stance of supporting and defending Secretary Lutnick. While noting there is no evidence that these investments by Cantor Fitzgerald influenced Secretary Lutnick's decision-making, the NYT highlighted that the relationship between Cantor Fitzgerald and the Southeast Asian data centers "illustrates a potential conflict of interest given the role Secretary Lutnick plays in shaping export-related regulations." The Trump administration has previously engaged in internal debates over the scope of semiconductor sales regulations targeting data centers in Southeast Asia.

While hardliners view such data centers as a loophole bypassing export bans to China, Secretary Lutnick has been known to oppose overly restricting U.S. companies like Nvidia from selling semiconductors to Asia.

Secretary Lutnick has reportedly delayed or suspended such export restrictions and controls over the past year on multiple occasions, arguing that they could negatively impact Nvidia or U.S.-China trade relations.
In particular, sources told the NYT that the Commerce Department has been pushing for a version that significantly scales back the scope of these export restrictions and controls.

According to reports, the plans involve applying regulations only to a select few countries—such as Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, South Africa, and Norway—applying them solely to cutting-edge semiconductors shipped going forward, and exempting data centers already built with U.S. technology from regulatory targets.
Amid this situation, Secretary Lutnick has found himself cornered following the eruption of a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

U.S. internet media outlet Axios noted, "Secretary Lutnick has become a symbol of the Trump administration's lackluster response to Chinese espionage activities and potential national security threats," adding, "The strongest criticisms are coming from Republican lawmakers, fellow cabinet members, and MAGA, President Trump's core support base." Ultimately, individuals around President Trump and within the Republican Party also want Secretary Lutnick to take responsibility for this crisis.

However, President Trump is reportedly maintaining his stance of supporting and defending Secretary Lutnick. (Photo: AP, Yonhap News) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.

extraction.body: The commerce secretary has been writing new rules that would affect Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of his former firm. Ana Swanson reported from Washington, Aaron Krolik from New York and Paul Mozur from Taiwan. In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers. The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms. The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business. Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A.I. computing power to Chinese firms. The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A.I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia. Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U.S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia.
On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centres as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban.
On the other are officials, most prominently Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of US companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia.

Lutnick steered Cantor Fitzgerald for decades, before recusing himself when he joined the Trump administration last year.
The Commerce Department says Lutnick has complied with all ethics agreements, and his former business is now run by his sons.
These dealings are just a tiny portion of Cantor’s business, which stretches from investment banking and trading to real estate.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump (left) and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick An investment firm founded by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has close ties to a Southeast Asian AI data center operator capable of supplying cutting-edge artificial intelligence semiconductor technology to China while bypassing U.S. regulations, The New York Times (NYT) reported on the 15th local time. The controversy surrounding Secretary Lutnick, who is at the center of suspicions over delays and suspensions in the Trump administration's export controls on advanced semiconductors to China due to the "Jensen Huang scandal," appears to be expanding into allegations of pursuing private interests. According to the NYT report, Bitdeer, a Singaporean company operating an AI data center named "A201" in southern Malaysia set to open next year, is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, a financial services firm founded by Secretary Lutnick and currently run by his son. Cantor Fitzgerald participated as a designated sales agent when Bitdeer carried out a stock offering worth up to $1 billion this year. In 2024 as well, Cantor Fitzgerald helped arrange a stock offering for Bitdeer valued at up to $250 million. This business structure is both legal and highly profitable. It also allows for circumventing U.S. regulations that ban the sale of cutting-edge AI semiconductors to Chinese companies. The NYT pointed out that beyond this, Cantor Fitzgerald has maintained business relationships with several data center companies in Southeast Asia targeting Chinese clients, which could be affected by regulations currently being prepared by the Commerce Department under Secretary Lutnick. While noting there is no evidence that these investments by Cantor Fitzgerald influenced Secretary Lutnick's decision-making, the NYT highlighted that the relationship between Cantor Fitzgerald and the Southeast Asian data centers "illustrates a potential conflict of interest given the role Secretary Lutnick plays in shaping export-related regulations." The Trump administration has previously engaged in internal debates over the scope of semiconductor sales regulations targeting data centers in Southeast Asia. While hardliners view such data centers as a loophole bypassing export bans to China, Secretary Lutnick has been known to oppose overly restricting U.S. companies like Nvidia from selling semiconductors to Asia. Secretary Lutnick has reportedly delayed or suspended such export restrictions and controls over the past year on multiple occasions, arguing that they could negatively impact Nvidia or U.S.-China trade relations. In particular, sources told the NYT that the Commerce Department has been pushing for a version that significantly scales back the scope of these export restrictions and controls. According to reports, the plans involve applying regulations only to a select few countries—such as Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, South Africa, and Norway—applying them solely to cutting-edge semiconductors shipped going forward, and exempting data centers already built with U.S. technology from regulatory targets. Amid this situation, Secretary Lutnick has found himself cornered following the eruption of a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. U.S. internet media outlet Axios noted, "Secretary Lutnick has become a symbol of the Trump administration's lackluster response to Chinese espionage activities and potential national security threats," adding, "The strongest criticisms are coming from Republican lawmakers, fellow cabinet members, and MAGA, President Trump's core support base." Ultimately, individuals around President Trump and within the Republican Party also want Secretary Lutnick to take responsibility for this crisis. However, President Trump is reportedly maintaining his stance of supporting and defending Secretary Lutnick.
