extraction.body: This was the first total mission failure in United Launch Alliance’s 20-year history. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry. The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time. Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights. Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC). In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.” “ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.” Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said. “ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.” The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred. Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem. Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds. Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance. A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course. ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin. Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon. First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity. Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers. Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. “There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.” Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana. Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time. What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year. That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’s chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement. It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads. Vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA. Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit. But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years. Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure. NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028. “Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.” Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.

Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’s chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

Vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

United Launch Alliance said its Vulcan vehicle suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit during the Amazon Leo 1 launch from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. The Vulcan malfunctioned during the climb to space on Sunday, dooming the 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites and throwing a costly wrench into both companies' launch schedules.

The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC). ULA said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred,” and it said engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.”

ULA said it would work with Amazon and other organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible, while it also said it did not yet have “any specific data to understand what occurred today.” Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” and it added that “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon.”

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman offered assistance, writing on X, “The team at @NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort.” ULA officials told reporters they would work closely with Amazon and other organizations, and it quoted ULA’s media update that “Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something.”

ULA said the anomaly would likely force a potentially significant grounding while engineers review telemetry and implement fixes for whatever caused the mishap, and it said it would return to flight as quickly as possible. Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan flights purchased by Amazon to launch its Leo satellites, and the failure would require Amazon Leo to wait on ULA’s failure investigation before trying again with a Vulcan.

Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025, and the last successful launch was in July when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5 rocket. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.
Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday.

For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.
Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.
That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit.

extraction.body: This was the first total mission failure in United Launch Alliance’s 20-year history. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry. The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time. Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. passages: This was the first total mission failure in United Launch Alliance’s 20-year history.

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).

In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”

“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”
Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said.

“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”
The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.

Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.

Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.
Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.

A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.

ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.
Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.

First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.

The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.

Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’s chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

Vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”

Here’s how it works . United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an anomaly during its launch today (Nov. 15), resulting in the loss of 40 Amazon internet satellites. The Vulcan Centaur lifted off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station today at 12:40 p.m. ET (1740 GMT), hauling 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation toward low Earth orbit (LEO). But they never got there. "Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in an update on X today , 50 minutes after launch. "Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today." Today's launch was supposed to be a bounce-back mission for the Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and had four total flights under its belt before today. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024 , and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs). In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addressed the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.) ULA worked hard on that front and got Vulcan ready to return to flight, which finally occurred today after nine months.. "The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update . That nozzle work apparently paid off: The SRBs appeared to perform as expected during today's launch. But a different, more serious problem cropped up today, and Vulcan Centaur could not overcome it. Today's launch was supposed to help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in LEO, which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years. Amazon Leo will consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Before today, about 400 of them had reached space on 15 launches, which were conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6 . Today's launch was the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1. The Amazon Leo launch was part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that featured the first-ever catch of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit. United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an anomaly during its launch today (Nov. 15), resulting in the loss of 40 Amazon internet satellites.

The Vulcan Centaur lifted off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station today at 12:40 p.m. ET (1740 GMT), hauling 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation toward low Earth orbit (LEO). But they never got there.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in an update on X today , 50 minutes after launch. "Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today."
Today's launch was supposed to be a bounce-back mission for the Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket.

Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and had four total flights under its belt before today. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024 , and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).

In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addressed the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)
ULA worked hard on that front and got Vulcan ready to return to flight, which finally occurred today after nine months..

"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update .
That nozzle work apparently paid off: The SRBs appeared to perform as expected during today's launch. But a different, more serious problem cropped up today, and Vulcan Centaur could not overcome it.

Today's launch was supposed to help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in LEO, which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.

Amazon Leo will consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Before today, about 400 of them had reached space on 15 launches, which were conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6 . Today's launch was the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.

The Amazon Leo launch was part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that featured the first-ever catch of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.
Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 15 with news of liftoff, then again at 1:45 p.m. ET with news of the anomaly and loss of the mission.

extraction.body: "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."It was only the fifth flight of a Vulcan rocket and the first in nine months as ULA and booster-supplier Northrop Grumman worked to resolve problems with nozzles used by strap-on solid-fuel boosters that marred two earlier flights.The solids appeared to work normally Sunday, helping boost the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere before burning out and falling away. The two methane-burning BE-4 engines powering the Vulcan's first stage then continued the climb toward orbit, but they appeared to fire longer than expected based on ULA's pre-launch timeline.After stage separation, the Vulcan's hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage engines took over for a planned 12-minute and 15-second burn. According to ULA's update, something went wrong during that Centaur firing, but no additional details were immediately provided.Sunday's launch was the first of 38 Vulcan flights purchased by Amazon to launch its Leo satellites, designed to compete head-to-head with Elon Musk's Starlink and other space-based internet providers. ULA has already launched eight Leo flights using Atlas 5 rockets.Amazon has also booked 24 Leo launches aboard Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, 24 aboard the European Ariane 6, and 13 aboard SpaceX's Falcon 9. More than 3,300 Leo satellites will be needed to complete the constellation. Sunday's flight would have pushed the total number launched to date to 436.But it was not to be.Instead, Amazon Leo will now have to wait on ULA's failure investigation to run its course before trying again with a Vulcan. The company also is waiting for Jeff Bezos-owned Blue Origin to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after a catastrophic on-pad explosion last May.That failure was caused by a problem with an oxygen valve in one of New Glenn's seven BE-4 first-stage engines. The BE-4, also built by Blue Origin, powers the Vulcan's first stage, but the engines used Sunday had been retrofitted with a fix by Blue Origin engineers.While the cause of the failure is not yet publicly known, "ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action," the company said.NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman promised assistance if needed."Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed," Isaacman wrote on the social media platform X. "The team at @NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. We are in your corner and here to help."The 214-foot-tall Vulcan blasted off from pad 41 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET, thundering away on a northeasterly trajectory atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust from six Northrop Grumman strap-on solid-fuel boosters and two methane-burning BE-4s.A launch attempt Friday was scrubbed after problems knocked out a gaseous nitrogen plant that serves multiple launch providers. Another delay was ordered Saturday because of network problems between the Vulcan and ground systems.On Sunday, launch controllers called a hold at the T-minus 20-second mark because of an unexplained technical issue with the rocket. Re-targeting the end of the launch window, ULA resolved the problem, and the rocket roared to life and climbed away at the end of the launch window.It's not yet known if the problem that interrupted the countdown played any role in the subsequent failure.In any case, the strap-on boosters helped propel the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere, burning out and falling away about a minute and 40 seconds after liftoff. But the first stage appeared to burn longer than called for in the company's pre-launch timeline.The first stage also appeared to separate from the rocket's hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage later than expected, and telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in the burn.ULA's launch commentators, however, did not mention any problems and the launch broadcast came to an end without confirming whether the Centaur's first planned engine firing went for the full duration.ULA spent months working to resolve problems with the strap-on booster nozzles that occurred during two earlier flights, one in 2024 and the other this past February. While ULA was free to proceed with commercial flights, the U.S. Space Force put Vulcan launches of national security payloads on hold pending further analysis."We've identified three credible causes (of the nozzle issue), and we have taken positive steps to mitigate all of those," ULA CEO Mark Peller told Aviation Week & Space Technology magazine in a pre-flight interview.The boosters appeared to work normally Sunday.As for the BE-4 engines, Peller said Blue Origin developed a "design improvement" to resolve the valve issue and carried out a "retrofit" on the engines installed on the Vulcan Leo 1 rocket."They were down at our facilities probably a couple months ago and implemented that retrofit kit on the engines on this upcoming mission," Peller said. "And they're working with us to work through our inventory of engines."

sources.title: Apple’s new study looks to improve the effectiveness of AI health tools
passages: Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are.

Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” said Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.
The aim is to improve the design and functionality of AI-powered health tools so they can deliver relevant health information that’s easier for users to understand and act on.

The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine.
The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute.
But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure users’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models.
Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources.
Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life.

extraction.body: The world of health care disruption and innovation often seems like a sprint, but it is a marathon. Apple is a perfect illustration. The tech giant recently announced its new wide-ranging Apple Health Study . The longitudinal research aims to further understand how technology can play a role in improving physical and mental health and overall well-being. The company stated that the study may take at least five years before its full impact is realized and will build on previous research from the Apple Women’s Study , Apple Hearing Study and the Apple Heart and Movement Study . Even with that lag time, results from the study have the potential to be groundbreaking, the company notes. Consumers can volunteer for the latest study through the Research app in the company’s iPhone and can opt out at any time. De-identified data from the study will explore relationships within various areas of health, such as mental health’s impact on heart rate or how sleep can influence exercise. The study is being conducted in collaboration with Brigham and Women’s Hospital, a research hospital and teaching affiliate of Harvard Medical School, Boston. Unlike prior Apple health studies that focused on specific areas, this research will gather data from iPhones, Apple Watches and AirPods to try to discover new relationships within different areas of health, both physical and mental. Much like its previous health studies, Apple will use the findings from this research to learn and inform its product development and potential features to add in the future. The hearing test offered through Apple’s AirPods is an example of how previous studies impacted product development. Other advances that came out of Apple research studies include the Vitals app on the AppleWatch and the Walking Steadiness app on the iPhone. Changes in health can affect one or more parts of the body, and others may affect well-being overall, so helping to identify these changes earlier can help offer a more proactive approach to health. For example, early detection of a change in hearing health could reduce the risk for cognitive decline. Study participants not only will contribute data but also will be prompted to answer questions periodically about their at-home life and habits. The study spans many health and disease areas, including activity, aging, cardiovascular health, circulatory health, cognition, hearing, menstrual health, mental health, metabolic health, mobility, neurologic health, respiratory health, sleep and more. The longitudinal, virtual study data can be used to predict, detect, monitor and manage changes in participants’ health, Apple states. Additionally, researchers will explore connections across different areas of health. It’s impossible to predict how many consumers will participate in the new Apple Health Study, but the company previously has had great success in recruiting participants for its research. More than 400,000 people participated in the first Apple Heart Study. Broadening the scope and scale of this study has the potential to reveal previously unknown connections between lifestyles and different areas of health. Access to a huge and diverse cohort (Apple device users) could help accelerate discovery and progress. “We anticipate we will likely find some signals that have previously just been missed because we haven’t had studies that are this broad, or we haven’t had studies that are this continuous. We haven’t looked longitudinally or at this level of granularity,” Calum MacRae, a cardiologist and professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, who will serve as principal investigator on the Apple Health Study, noted in a recent interview . sources.title: Apple seeks up to 200,000 U.S. participants for AI health study - Inquisitr
passages: Apple launched a research app Sunday that answers health questions with artificial intelligence, seeking up to 200,000 U.S. participants to examine how people use and trust AI health advice.
The Apple Health AI Usage Study, developed with clinical AI company OpenEvidence, accepts U.S. residents who are 21 or older.
Its answers use clinical sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature, with links to peer-reviewed citations for each response.
"Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life," Dr.
Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement.
Apple created the study experience, using its technology to translate OpenEvidence's research into answers intended to be easy to understand.
Only health care professionals currently have full access to the OpenEvidence platform.
Apple said the iPhone processes each query first, removing identifying details before OpenEvidence receives it.
The company said OpenEvidence deletes question-and-response data within 24 hours and that study data will not train AI models.
"When people have access to clear, medically grounded information, they can walk into their doctor's appointments feeling more prepared, informed, and confident," Desai told ABC News.
The study does not provide live medical monitoring, diagnosis or treatment, and is no substitute for a health care professional.
Whether Apple plans to bring AI-powered answers to its Health app or Siri is unclear.

Apple launched a research app Sunday that answers health questions with artificial intelligence, seeking up to 200,000 U.S. participants to examine how people use and trust AI health advice. The Apple Health AI Usage Study, developed with clinical AI company OpenEvidence, accepts U.S. residents who are 21 or older. Its answers use clinical sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature, with links to peer-reviewed citations for each response. "Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life," Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement. Earlier research found a gap between chatbot performance and users' ability to reach correct answers. In a February 2026 Oxford study published in Nature Medicine, chatbots identified conditions in clinical cases nearly 95% of the time, ABC News reported. Everyday users reached the correct answer less than 35% of the time. "Millions of people are turning to AI for health advice, but accurate answers aren't always useful," said Dr. John Brownstein, an ABC News contributor and professor at Harvard Medical School in pediatrics and biomedical informatics. "Confusing or incomplete information can create false reassurance or delay care," he said. Apple created the study experience, using its technology to translate OpenEvidence's research into answers intended to be easy to understand. Only health care professionals currently have full access to the OpenEvidence platform. Participants can opt to provide HealthKit information, including resting heart rate, activity, sleep or lab results, for answers tailored more closely to them. A person seeking to improve their resting heart rate, for example, could get advice based on their measurements instead of general recommendations. The app uses text prompts and has no Siri or Apple Intelligence integration, although users can dictate through the iOS keyboard, The Verge reported. Participants assess responses on criteria that include accuracy and relevance. To enroll, participants go through onboarding with informed consent and are asked for demographic details, including age and education. They can comment on answers and receive surveys during the study. Apple said the iPhone processes each query first, removing identifying details before OpenEvidence receives it. The company said OpenEvidence deletes question-and-response data within 24 hours and that study data will not train AI models. The App Store privacy label separately says identifiers may be collected and linked to a user's identity for analytics and app functionality, Unite.AI reported. The app includes safeguards intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest follow-up with a provider or other resources. The study does not provide live medical monitoring, diagnosis or treatment, and is no substitute for a health care professional. Its answers use clinical sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature, with links to peer-reviewed citations for each response.

"Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life," Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement.

Earlier research found a gap between chatbot performance and users' ability to reach correct answers. In a February 2026 Oxford study published in Nature Medicine, chatbots identified conditions in clinical cases nearly 95% of the time, ABC News reported. Everyday users reached the correct answer less than 35% of the time.

"Millions of people are turning to AI for health advice, but accurate answers aren't always useful," said Dr. John Brownstein, an ABC News contributor and professor at Harvard Medical School in pediatrics and biomedical informatics. "Confusing or incomplete information can create false reassurance or delay care," he said.

Apple created the study experience, using its technology to translate OpenEvidence's research into answers intended to be easy to understand. Only health care professionals currently have full access to the OpenEvidence platform.

Participants can opt to provide HealthKit information, including resting heart rate, activity, sleep or lab results, for answers tailored more closely to them. A person seeking to improve their resting heart rate, for example, could get advice based on their measurements instead of general recommendations.

Additionally, researchers will explore connections across different areas of health. Broadening the scope and scale of this study has the potential to reveal previously unknown connections between lifestyles and different areas of health. sources.title: Apple seeks up to 200,000 U.S. participants for AI health study - Inquisitr
passages: Apple launched a research app Sunday that answers health questions with artificial intelligence, seeking up to 200,000 U.S. participants to examine how people use and trust AI health advice.
The Apple Health AI Usage Study, developed with clinical AI company OpenEvidence, accepts U.S. residents who are 21 or older.
Its answers use clinical sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature, with links to peer-reviewed citations for each response.
"Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life," Dr.
Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement.
Apple created the study experience, using its technology to translate OpenEvidence's research into answers intended to be easy to understand.
Only health care professionals currently have full access to the OpenEvidence platform.
Apple said the iPhone processes each query first, removing identifying details before OpenEvidence receives it.
The company said OpenEvidence deletes question-and-response data within 24 hours and that study data will not train AI models.
"When people have access to clear, medically grounded information, they can walk into their doctor's appointments feeling more prepared, informed, and confident," Desai told ABC News.
The study does not provide live medical monitoring, diagnosis or treatment, and is no substitute for a health care professional.
Whether Apple plans to bring AI-powered answers to its Health app or Siri is unclear.

extraction.body: U.S. residents 21 and older can join the study, whose app links answers to peer-reviewed clinical sources. Apple launched a research app Sunday that answers health questions with artificial intelligence, seeking up to 200,000 U.S. participants to examine how people use and trust AI health advice. The Apple Health AI Usage Study, developed with clinical AI company OpenEvidence, accepts U.S. residents who are 21 or older. Its answers use clinical sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature, with links to peer-reviewed citations for each response. "Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life," Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement. Earlier research found a gap between chatbot performance and users' ability to reach correct answers. In a February 2026 Oxford study published in Nature Medicine, chatbots identified conditions in clinical cases nearly 95% of the time, ABC News reported. Everyday users reached the correct answer less than 35% of the time. "Millions of people are turning to AI for health advice, but accurate answers aren't always useful," said Dr. John Brownstein, an ABC News contributor and professor at Harvard Medical School in pediatrics and biomedical informatics. "Confusing or incomplete information can create false reassurance or delay care," he said. Apple created the study experience, using its technology to translate OpenEvidence's research into answers intended to be easy to understand. Only health care professionals currently have full access to the OpenEvidence platform. Participants can opt to provide HealthKit information, including resting heart rate, activity, sleep or lab results, for answers tailored more closely to them. A person seeking to improve their resting heart rate, for example, could get advice based on their measurements instead of general recommendations. The app uses text prompts and has no Siri or Apple Intelligence integration, although users can dictate through the iOS keyboard, The Verge reported. Participants assess responses on criteria that include accuracy and relevance. To enroll, participants go through onboarding with informed consent and are asked for demographic details, including age and education. They can comment on answers and receive surveys during the study. Apple said the iPhone processes each query first, removing identifying details before OpenEvidence receives it. The company said OpenEvidence deletes question-and-response data within 24 hours and that study data will not train AI models. The App Store privacy label separately says identifiers may be collected and linked to a user's identity for analytics and app functionality, Unite.AI reported. The app includes safeguards intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest follow-up with a provider or other resources. The study does not provide live medical monitoring, diagnosis or treatment, and is no substitute for a health care professional. "When people have access to clear, medically grounded information, they can walk into their doctor's appointments feeling more prepared, informed, and confident," Desai told ABC News. Apple said the research is intended to inform responsible health AI design at Apple and across the industry, and it plans to make the findings broadly available. "We're collecting enormous amounts of personal health data through phones and wearables, but turning that information into something people can actually understand and act on remains a challenge," Brownstein said. Whether Apple plans to bring AI-powered answers to its Health app or Siri is unclear. OpenAI and Anthropic already offer chatbot features tailored to health questions. Earlier in 2026, OpenAI said users were asking more than 300 million health-related questions each week .

extraction.body: Calls for governments to recognise sexual exploitation of children as preventable public health emergency Calls for governments to recognise sexual exploitation of children as preventable public health emergency Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found. A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025. The images, although fake, can be used to blackmail children to demand money or more images. The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the US-based organisation the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children . Prof Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight, said the findings showed the “shocking” level of child sexual exploitation. The research focuses on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Previous studies have examined western Europe. Fry said: “Our research reveals the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and abuse and how rapidly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online. “But the findings also show where governments can make a difference. By bringing together evidence from surveys, police records and other sources, we can build a clearer picture of the risks children face, identify weaknesses in protection systems and help target resources and interventions where they are needed most.” A report by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) last month found AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online , with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025. IWF analysts have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the previous year. The UK-based NGO, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500. The problem had already risen in 2025, according to the IWF. Childlight estimates more than 300 million children worldwide are the victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse ever year. It also estimates that about one in four children will be subjected to at least one form of abuse before their 18th birthday. The research also looked at offline sexual abuse reporting. Almost a third of girls, and more than one in 10 boys were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood in North America, the research found. This includes crimes such as sexual assault, rape and “upskirting”. The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada. Fry said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years. “While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.” Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk. “We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature. Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found.

A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.
The images, although fake, can be used to blackmail children to demand money or more images.
The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the US-based organisation the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children .
Prof Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight, said the findings showed the “shocking” level of child sexual exploitation.
The research focuses on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Previous studies have examined western Europe.
Fry said: “Our research reveals the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and abuse and how rapidly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online.

“But the findings also show where governments can make a difference. By bringing together evidence from surveys, police records and other sources, we can build a clearer picture of the risks children face, identify weaknesses in protection systems and help target resources and interventions where they are needed most.”

A report by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) last month found AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online , with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.

IWF analysts have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the previous year. The UK-based NGO, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.
The problem had already risen in 2025, according to the IWF.
Childlight estimates more than 300 million children worldwide are the victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse ever year.
It also estimates that about one in four children will be subjected to at least one form of abuse before their 18th birthday. The research also looked at offline sexual abuse reporting.

Almost a third of girls, and more than one in 10 boys were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood in North America, the research found. This includes crimes such as sexual assault, rape and “upskirting”.
The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada.

Fry said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.

“While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.”

Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk.

“We are calling on governments to recognise this as a preventable public health emergency, invest in better evidence and turn that intelligence into action. Of 103 countries and areas examined across the three regions, the group said only 22 had representative survey data covering both offline and technology-facilitated abuse.

The institute is also calling for stronger technology-sector accountability, laws that keep pace with emerging threats and prevention efforts beginning earlier in childhood.

extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. A deputy working security at a South Carolina gun and knife show fatally shot a customer who opened fire at him, according to authorities. The unidentified deputy was shot by Telvin Pierre Portee, 34, at the South Carolina Arms Collectors Association show in the Jamil Temple on Saturday afternoon, according to the Lexington County Sheriff’s Office. The cop, who was working security at the event, returned fire and struck the gun-wielding patron, police said. Portee, of Columbia, died at the scene from a gunshot wound, according to the Lexington County Coroner’s Office. The deputy was rushed to the hospital, where he underwent surgery. He is in stable condition, cops said. It is not immediately known what sparked the gunfire between him and Portee. The SCACA canceled the gun and knife show slated to run on Saturday and Sunday at the Jamil Temple, which supports Shriners Children’s Hospitals, following the deadly shootout. “Due to today’s unfortunate circumstances,” the organization said in a social media post , “the SCACA Gun & Knife Show will be canceled for Sunday, November 15. We sincerely apologize for any inconvenience and appreciate your understanding.” The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division will investigate the shooting.

The candidate, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam, admitted via his lawyer that he photographed questions with a miniature camera, sent them to AI for answers, and viewed the results on his smartphone. This case adds to growing concerns about high-tech cheating methods, following recent incidents involving smart glasses in other certifications and upcoming plans to address similar issues in the national university entrance exam. South Korean police said Sunday they had launched an investigation after the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam admitted to using artificial intelligence to cheat. The candidate, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam held in April and July, confessed through his lawyer that he used AI to obtain answers during the tests. His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.“We received a written confession through the test taker’s lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam,” the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency said, adding the case had been assigned to investigators. In a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the candidate said he “deeply regretted” what he had done.“I used a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions and sent them to AI, then checked the answers on my smartphone,” he said. “I wanted to make money, and I hated seeing myself disappointing my parents after quitting a good job,” he said. The examination is administered by the Human Resources Development Service of Korea , which said two supervisors were present when the candidate sat the test.The HRDK said Sunday an “AI inspector” caught a test taker wearing smart glasses during a gas engineer certification exam last month. In October, the government announced plans to file criminal complaints against students caught using such devices in the national university entrance exam. With the annual college entrance test, known as the “Suneung”, due to take place on November 19, the presidential office said it was treating the issue seriously.The presidential office “has been working hard to come up with measures to address it,” chief of staff Lim Kwang-hyun told reporters.“A meeting to discuss those measures will be held this afternoon, chaired by the presidential chief of staff for policy, and preparations are underway,” he added.

Han, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam held in April and July, confessed through his lawyer that he used AI to obtain answers during the tests. He said he had cheated by ‌taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.
His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.

It comes just days before Thursday’s annual national college entrance exam, ‌a high-pressure event for which many South ​Korean students will have spent much of their lives preparing.

“The presidential office views ​the matter very seriously, and because the college entrance exam is next week, we have been working hard to prepare countermeasures,” a senior presidential office official told reporters on Sunday.

The official said reports of potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam were concerning, adding ⁠that the presidential chief of staff for policy would convene an emergency meeting later ​in the afternoon to ​address the issue.

The prime minister, Han Seong-sook, acknowledged on Friday public concerns over AI-assisted cheating. The government would “prepare thoroughly in advance and closely oversee the process until the very end to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted fairly and stably”, a statement from her office said.

extraction.body: Ethereum's slide to its weakest level since July has set off a public clash between two of the asset's most vocal camps, with gold advocate Peter Schiff predicting a further collapse toward $1,000 and BitMine chairman Tom Lee insisting the pressure will pass. Schiff said in a post on X on Saturday that a weekend break of support around $1,600 could deliver a "Black Monday" for BitMine (BMNR) and Ethereum ETFs, sending ETH to $1,000 by the start of the trading week. "It's not too late to sell," he told holders. The token had already lost more than 8% since his first warning. Lee, who chairs the largest corporate holder of the asset, responded the same day by saying the strain on crypto prices would ease and repeating his view of ETH as "the future of finance." Ethereum changed hands near $1,830 on Sunday, roughly 18% lower over seven days and about 25% weaker over the past month. It touched a low of about $1,710 to $1,713 over the weekend, the softest print since July, before rebounding around 4% in 24 hours. Bitcoin slipped about 2.5% to near $65,500. The dispute matters most for BitMine, which disclosed holdings of about 6.07 million ETH as of Nov. 8, acquired at an average of $2,234 per coin. At Sunday's price, the position carries an unrealized loss of roughly $2.5 billion, or about 18% below cost. The company's shares fell about 6.3% on the day. Note: Prices and holdings figures reflect the most recent disclosures cited in weekend market coverage. Schiff's track record on the coin is uneven. In April 2025 he forecast that ETH would fall below $1,000; instead it rallied to a record $4,954 on Aug. 24, 2025. Technical gauges offer little comfort to either side. ETH trades far beneath its 50-day and 200-day moving averages, which have converged just above $2,280 and now form a single thick ceiling over the price. The daily relative strength index sits near 26, below the 30 threshold that marks oversold conditions, while the MACD remains under its signal line and trend readings continue to favor sellers. That combination suggests the market is stretched to the downside without having turned. Bounces in such setups frequently stall before reaching the key averages, and the weekend rally has recovered only a fraction of the month's decline. The nearest mapped support is the weekend low near $1,710. A clean break would leave little in the way of a floor until Schiff's $1,600 line and then this year's lowest daily close of $1,566 on June 26, a zone buyers defended once before. To the upside, resistance waits near $2,170; a close above it would be the first meaningful sign of repair, with the merged averages forming the next hurdle. A close above resistance would open a path toward the moving averages, ease pressure on BitMine and push Schiff's warning aside, though that view fails if ETH drops back under the weekend low. A daily close below that floor would leave little support ahead of the $1,600 level and the June low close behind it. For investors, the immediate risk runs through the same support level both men are debating. Further weakness would deepen BitMine's paper losses and could prompt fresh selling from the largest corporate holder, adding momentum to any decline. A sustained reclaim of resistance would instead shift attention back to whether corporate treasuries can weather a prolonged drawdown in the asset they have accumulated most heavily. Lee, who chairs the largest corporate holder of the asset, responded the same day by saying the strain on crypto prices would ease and repeating his view of ETH as "the future of finance." Ethereum changed hands near $1,830 on Sunday, roughly 18% lower over seven days and about 25% weaker over the past month. It touched a low of about $1,710 to $1,713 over the weekend, the softest print since July, before rebounding around 4% in 24 hours. Bitcoin slipped about 2.5% to near $65,500. The dispute matters most for BitMine, which disclosed holdings of about 6.07 million ETH as of Nov. 8, acquired at an average of $2,234 per coin. extraction.body: Peter Schiff, chief economist and global strategist at Euro Pacific Capital, warned that Ether ETH could fall to $1,000 by Monday if it breaks below $1,600 over the weekend, following steep losses across cryptocurrency markets. “Remember this warning from twelve hours ago? Ethereum is already over 8% lower. It's not too late to sell,” Schiff wrote on X. “If Ether breaks $1,600 this weekend, it could crash to $1,000 on Monday. That really would be a Black Monday for Ethereum ETFs and $BMNR.” BMNR BMNR is the ticker for Bitmine Immersion Technologies, a company focused on building an Ether treasury. The warning followed a Nov. 14 post in which Schiff outlined a bearish interpretation of Ethereum’s chart. “It's not just Bitcoin that's about to crash. Check out Ethereum. That chart looks even more ominous,” he wrote. “Once it breaks the uptrend at around $1,600, the next support level is the 2022 low just below $1,000.” Ether fell 8.27% on Saturday to $1,769.82 after losing 4.47% on Friday. Investing.com’s Sunday snapshot showed a partial recovery to $1,807.60, with an intraday low of $1,713.57, still above Schiff’s $1,600 threshold. Bitcoin BTCUSD fell 6.06% on Saturday to $64,145.30 after dropping 4.4% on Friday. Its Sunday snapshot showed a 1.23% recovery to $64,932.50. Both cryptocurrencies remained below their Nov. 9 levels of $2,135.12 for Ether and $75,330.60 for Bitcoin. Schiff also highlighted the constraints facing Bitcoin ETF investors during a weekend selloff. “The people who self-custody Bitcoin are lucky. They can sell anytime they want to. They don't have to slowly watch the value of their Bitcoin melt away. They can sell now. But owners of Bitcoin ETFs have to watch helplessly until Monday morning to sell and salvage what's left,” he wrote. Bitcoin trades around the clock, allowing direct holders to seek buyers over the weekend. ETF shareholders face trading schedules that can leave them unable to sell while the underlying cryptocurrency falls. Schiff’s Monday-morning claim has exceptions: some brokers offer overnight trading in eligible ETFs beginning Sunday evening, depending on the security. Still, ETF investors can face gaps in trading access while Bitcoin’s price continues to move.
