sources.title: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
passages: Bharat Semi , an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China.
The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub.
The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors.
The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added.
The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software.
The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.
Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.
Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara.
It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.
The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.
Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace.

Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors.

The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

extraction.body: Bharat Semi , an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere. The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027. India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets. The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview. “Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch. Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision. Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system. The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027. The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market. Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe. “It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said. In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility. The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility. passages: TechTimes views the $24 million seed round as a pivotal moment for India's semiconductor ambitions, especially as Bharat Semi targets AI‑enabled image sensors that could dramatically lower system costs.
If the company meets its 2027 production timeline, it may secure a foothold in U.S. defense and consumer markets, offering a home‑grown alternative to Chinese supply chains.
However, its fabless model means reliance on external foundries, which could expose the venture to global capacity constraints as the industry continues to diversify manufacturing locations.
The all‑equity round was led by Info Edge Group , South Park Commons and Indus Bridge Ventures , with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels and several individual investors.
The capital will fund an expansion of the engineering team, finalise product development and bring the sensors to market.
Bharat Semi now employs roughly 75 people across India and the United States, including 10‑12 staff in Santa Clara, and plans to grow the U.S. headcount to about 20 by mid‑2027.
The initiative remains in the planning phase and is separate from the image‑sensor business; Bharat Semi will stay fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on design and software.
The new seed funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.
Bharat Semi was founded in late 2021 by Vrinda Kapoor and Vinayak Dalmia .
Chief technology officer Boyd Fowler previously led the same function at OmniVision and now heads the chip design team.
The company is also hiring engineers in Europe to broaden its talent pool.

extraction.body: The crypto market ended Thursday night with its steepest daily loss in weeks. At 07:30 UTC on November 13, 2026, bitcoin traded at about $69,000, down a little over 6% in 24 hours, after touching an intraday low of $67,922 according to CoinGecko. Total crypto market capitalization fell about 7% over the same period to roughly $2.35 trillion. If you are asking why is crypto down today, our running explainer tracks every sell-off of the year. This crypto news roundup sets out what is driving the move: forced selling of leveraged positions, outflows from US spot bitcoin ETFs, a strong dollar with rising Treasury yields, and thin order books. Our first report with key price levels is Bitcoin price falls below $70,000. Crypto news at a glance: bitcoin, ether, BNB and XRP this morning Losses run through the large caps, but not evenly. As of 07:30 UTC, per CoinGecko data: Bitcoin: about $69,000, down 6.2% in 24 hours. According to CoinDesk, ether fell below $2,000 for the first time since August; see Ethereum price below $2,000. BNB: about $634, down 5.9%; more in BNB falls below $650. XRP: about $1.03, down 1.3%, with an intraday low just under $1. XRP and Solana fell less than bitcoin and ether over the past day, but both had already lost more earlier in the week: over seven days XRP is down a little over 14% and Solana just over 10%, per CoinGecko. For medium-term scenarios, see our bitcoin price prediction and ethereum price prediction. Liquidations: more than $1.3 billion in leveraged bets wiped out in 24 hours A liquidation is the forced closing of a leveraged position by an exchange once the posted collateral no longer covers it. Based on CoinGlass data analysed by CoinDesk early Friday, more than $1.3 billion in crypto futures were liquidated within 24 hours, about $677 million of them on bitcoin. The largest single liquidation was a long bitcoin position worth more than $31 million on Hyperliquid, according to the same report. Later snapshots reported by KuCoin News and Bloomingbit reached up to $1.62 billion. The defensible range is therefore $1.3 billion to $1.6 billion, most of it from traders who had bet on rising prices. Bitcoin ETF outflows: why US funds are weighing on the price The second driver is US fund flows. According to Cointelegraph, BlackRock's IBIT recorded more than $2 billion in net outflows over nine consecutive sessions through Wednesday. Across all US spot bitcoin ETFs, nearly $1.44 billion left over five sessions. Preliminary Farside data showed a further $47.7 million in net outflows on Thursday, with BlackRock and Fidelity figures still pending. When investors redeem shares, the fund generally has to sell bitcoin, which adds to the pressure from liquidations. Dollar and Treasury yields: the macro pressure on crypto CoinDesk points to a strong US dollar: the Dollar Index rose above 103, its highest since April 2025. After a hotter-than-expected October CPI reading, markets also raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Per Cointelegraph, data from 10x Research show bitcoin fell 5.9% between November 5 and 12, while the 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5%. Order book depth: why the bitcoin price swings so hard Order book depth measures how many buy and sell orders sit close to the current price. According to Talos, cited by Cointelegraph, bitcoin order book depth across major exchanges stood at $72 million on November 9, roughly 33% below normal. Talos senior research associate Tanay Ved said liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction. With few resting orders, even medium-sized sales trigger large price jumps. Fear and Greed Index at 20: extreme fear in the crypto market Sentiment matches the price action. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index from alternative.me reads 20 on Friday, which is "Extreme Fear", down from 28 the day before. Cointelegraph notes this is the lowest reading since July 8. CoinDesk also reported that the overnight sell-off accelerated on news of renewed military escalation in the Middle East. Bitcoin below $70,000: what US and UK investors should check now For readers in the United States, the IRS treats digital assets as property, so a sale at a loss is a capital loss that you report on your return. In the United Kingdom, the FCA warns that crypto is largely unregulated, that all cryptoassets are high risk, and that investors should be prepared to lose all their money.

passages: By John Meyer, consultant in finance and business – Eurasia Business News, November 15, 2026.
Cryptocurrency markets remained under pressure Sunday, November 15, as Bitcoin recovered from a sharp overnight decline while Ethereum, Solana and other major digital assets struggled to stabilize.

Bitcoin briefly traded near $62,000 before recovering toward $65,000, gaining +0.66% over the day, reflecting a volatile market shaped by institutional withdrawals, forced liquidations and expectations of higher U.S. interest rates.
Investors will watch whether Bitcoin’s rebound survives renewed selling, whether ETF withdrawals moderate and whether leveraged liquidations subside.
Expectations surrounding the Federal Reserve’s December policy meeting remain another source of uncertainty.
Meanwhile, the Crypto Fear & Greed Index fell to 12 on November 15 , classified as extreme fear.
That reading describes sentiment rather than proving that prices have bottomed.
U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded approximately $1.07 billion in net outflows during the latest trading week.
Bitcoin.com, citing SoSoValue, reported approximately $2.97 billion in withdrawals across 12 trading sessions ending November 13.
These are preceding trading-session flows, not Sunday ETF redemptions.
Bitcoin.com cited DefiLlama data showing approximately $284.85 billion outstanding on November 14, down 5.36% over 30 days.
Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC together accounted for $244.42 billion.
XRP attracted attention after falling below $1 and touching approximately $0.8922.
Eastern time, but the rebound followed prices last seen around November 2024.
The $1 threshold was psychologically important, although crossing it does not independently determine future direction.
Ethereum’s native asset, Ether, also experienced substantial volatility.
Investing.com reported an overnight low of $1,711 before a recovery toward $1,808 in its morning update.
The move left Ether below $2,000 despite a meaningful bounce from its weakest level.

passages: By John Meyer, consultant in finance and business – Eurasia Business News, November 15, 2026.

Bitcoin briefly traded near $62,000 before recovering toward $65,000, gaining +0.66% over the day, reflecting a volatile market shaped by institutional withdrawals, forced liquidations and expectations of higher U.S. interest rates.
Investors will watch whether Bitcoin’s rebound survives renewed selling, whether ETF withdrawals moderate and whether leveraged liquidations subside.
Expectations surrounding the Federal Reserve’s December policy meeting remain another source of uncertainty.

That reading describes sentiment rather than proving that prices have bottomed.
U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded approximately $1.07 billion in net outflows during the latest trading week.
Bitcoin.com, citing SoSoValue, reported approximately $2.97 billion in withdrawals across 12 trading sessions ending November 13.

Bitcoin.com cited DefiLlama data showing approximately $284.85 billion outstanding on November 14, down 5.36% over 30 days.
Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC together accounted for $244.42 billion.
XRP attracted attention after falling below $1 and touching approximately $0.8922.
Eastern time, but the rebound followed prices last seen around November 2024.
The $1 threshold was psychologically important, although crossing it does not independently determine future direction.
Ethereum’s native asset, Ether, also experienced substantial volatility.
Investing.com reported an overnight low of $1,711 before a recovery toward $1,808 in its morning update.
The move left Ether below $2,000 despite a meaningful bounce from its weakest level.

extraction.body: PARIS — France will test its artificial intelligence-powered battlefield command system with allies during a NATO interoperability exercise this month, as an alternative to the Maven Smart System developed by Palantir Technologies, said Gen. Patrick Justel, deputy chief of the French Army staff. The French have been developing the system with local companies including Mistral AI , Safran.AI , Thales and Airbus , Justel said in a media briefing on Thursday. The French Army has already tested the system, dubbed Arcadia, in exercises including Dacian Fall in Romania and Orion 26 in France. NATO military personnel started training with Palantir’s Maven Smart System in August 2025, the alliance’s first use of AI-enabled command and control software. The platform is derived from the Pentagon’s Project Maven and ties together massive amounts of battlefield data and AI analysis to help commanders identify targets and make decisions more quickly. Arcadia “is our response to Maven,” said Justel. He said NATO’s use of Maven raises issues of digital sovereignty, “so the question arises whether should we adopt Maven blindly, or should we look for other solutions.” France’s army, general staff and Defense Digital Commission “have been working on what other solutions might look like,” Justel said. France will deploy Arcadia during NATO’s Coalition Warrior Interoperability Exercise, or CWIX, a live exercise held in Poland June 8-26. Justel said several NATO countries including France have raised questions around interoperability with the Palantir system. The Army deputy chief of staff said Arcadia is designed to comply with NATO’s Federated Mission Networking standards, or FMN, and contrasted that with Maven, which he said hasn’t integrated FMN requirements. Palantir said Maven Smart System is “compliant with the principles of FMN” and that it is working with NATO toward official certification, in an emailed response to a request for comment. The company added that the platform has proven compliance with two NATO data-security standards that are “key building blocks” of FMN. “NATO Maven Smart System is compatible, and does allow interoperability, but of course nations are free to choose what systems they use,” said Martin O’Donnell, a spokesperson for Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers, in an emailed reply to questions. The Palantir system is already integrated with more than 10 NATO systems, according to U.S. Army Col. Arnel David, the director of Task Force Maven at SHAPE, who said his team is “focused on securing final certification across all FMN milestones,” with the declaration of full operational capability imminent. France plans to propose Arcadia to its European partners, with a number of countries expressing interest, and has organized demonstrations for NATO, which is also interested, the general said. “When we talk to our European partners, we get the same reaction of, `well, we’ve kind of gone with Maven because there’s no choice, but if countries in Europe are able to build an alternative, we’ll go for it.’” Palantir said it “welcomes the opportunity to integrate with Arcadia, or any other national system.” Arcadia builds on previous work by the Armed Forces Ministry as part of the Artemis project started in 2022, which uses AI to process massive amounts of defense data. The French Army has been developing use cases for Arcadia internally as well as in cooperation with the industry partners, according to Justel. The United Kingdom is working on a similar AI-enabled command and control system, and is also in discussions on how to interface with Maven, according to Justel. Based on discussions with the British, “their concept is well-established, but they don’t yet have all the technological building blocks,” said Col. Frédéric Vola, head of the planning and capacity development office in the Army general staff, in the briefing. While Palantir is behind the version of Maven used by NATO, the system is not the same as that used by the U.S., with different databases and functionality and “certainly not the same performance,” according to Justel. The French system is conceived to be a more resilient alternative to Maven because it will be “highly decentralized” rather than a centralized system, with all command posts connected to field-deployed servers in a mesh-network architecture rather than a distant central cloud. extraction.body: This week’s video takes viewers to Portugal’s Tróia Peninsula for REPMUS 2026, short for Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems. The Portuguese Navy led the annual exercise from 31 August to 25 September. NATO Channel describes it as “the ultimate testing ground for the future of robotic warfare at sea,” bringing together uncrewed surface vessels, underwater vehicles, aerial drones, artificial intelligence and advanced sensors ( DVIDS ). The film includes footage of the systems on display and interviews with three of the people behind the experiment: Justin Simmons of NATO’s Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA); Captain Sérgio Ricardo Caldeira de Carvalho, Director of the Portuguese Navy Operational Experimentation Centre (CEOM); and João Alves, Head of Experimentation and Exercise at the NATO Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation (CMRE). The central theme is interoperability: getting different uncrewed systems to communicate, share data and work together, while AI helps operators make decisions faster ( DVIDS ). According to NATO , REPMUS 2026 involved 300 uncrewed systems, 60 research and development companies and representatives of 36 navies. The Portuguese Navy ran it with the University of Porto’s engineering faculty, CMRE, NATO’s Joint Capability Group on Maritime Unmanned Systems and the European Defence Agency. One strand tested Task Force X-Arctic, an Allied Command Transformation project on how networked uncrewed systems can provide situational awareness across the North Atlantic, the Arctic and the High North. ACT says the month of trials showed the project can connect and orchestrate a wide range of autonomous systems from nations, industry and academia. For the Royal Navy, which led the operational scenarios, the focus was anti-submarine warfare. Gliders, squads of small and medium uncrewed surface vessels, and 12- and 17-metre autonomous boats were tested on towing sonar, dropping sonobuoys and launching gliders, in support of the Atlantic Bastion programme ( Ocean News ). The most important thing in this video is not any single drone. It is the connective tissue that lets many drones from many countries work as one force. Navies are now buying uncrewed systems faster than they are learning to integrate them. REPMUS is where that gap shows up and where allies try to close it before a crisis forces them to. This year’s work on letting a single operator control several different types of system through one common interface, reported by Daily Mare , is how a navy short of sailors gets more coverage without adding crews. The setting matters too. The same networked approach being tested off Portugal is aimed at the North Atlantic and the High North, where submarine activity and threats to seabed infrastructure put the greatest strain on allied navies. What the experiment shows is that systems can be connected and orchestrated. What it does not yet show is that this works at scale, over long periods and against a capable adversary. That is the next step, not this one. Note on figures: The video description and Navy Leaders report more than 1,500 personnel, while NATO’s news release gives more than 3,700 participants. NATO Channel describes it as “the ultimate testing ground for the future of robotic warfare at sea,” bringing together uncrewed surface vessels, underwater vehicles, aerial drones, artificial intelligence and advanced sensors ( DVIDS ). extraction.body: This week’s video takes viewers to Portugal’s Tróia Peninsula for REPMUS 2026, short for Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems. The Portuguese Navy led the annual exercise from 31 August to 25 September. NATO Channel describes it as “the ultimate testing ground for the future of robotic warfare at sea,” bringing together uncrewed surface vessels, underwater vehicles, aerial drones, artificial intelligence and advanced sensors ( DVIDS ). The film includes footage of the systems on display and interviews with three of the people behind the experiment: Justin Simmons of NATO’s Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA); Captain Sérgio Ricardo Caldeira de Carvalho, Director of the Portuguese Navy Operational Experimentation Centre (CEOM); and João Alves, Head of Experimentation and Exercise at the NATO Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation (CMRE). The central theme is interoperability: getting different uncrewed systems to communicate, share data and work together, while AI helps operators make decisions faster ( DVIDS ). According to NATO , REPMUS 2026 involved 300 uncrewed systems, 60 research and development companies and representatives of 36 navies. The Portuguese Navy ran it with the University of Porto’s engineering faculty, CMRE, NATO’s Joint Capability Group on Maritime Unmanned Systems and the European Defence Agency. One strand tested Task Force X-Arctic, an Allied Command Transformation project on how networked uncrewed systems can provide situational awareness across the North Atlantic, the Arctic and the High North. ACT says the month of trials showed the project can connect and orchestrate a wide range of autonomous systems from nations, industry and academia. For the Royal Navy, which led the operational scenarios, the focus was anti-submarine warfare. Gliders, squads of small and medium uncrewed surface vessels, and 12- and 17-metre autonomous boats were tested on towing sonar, dropping sonobuoys and launching gliders, in support of the Atlantic Bastion programme ( Ocean News ). The most important thing in this video is not any single drone. It is the connective tissue that lets many drones from many countries work as one force. Navies are now buying uncrewed systems faster than they are learning to integrate them. REPMUS is where that gap shows up and where allies try to close it before a crisis forces them to. This year’s work on letting a single operator control several different types of system through one common interface, reported by Daily Mare , is how a navy short of sailors gets more coverage without adding crews. The setting matters too. The same networked approach being tested off Portugal is aimed at the North Atlantic and the High North, where submarine activity and threats to seabed infrastructure put the greatest strain on allied navies. What the experiment shows is that systems can be connected and orchestrated. What it does not yet show is that this works at scale, over long periods and against a capable adversary. That is the next step, not this one. Note on figures: The video description and Navy Leaders report more than 1,500 personnel, while NATO’s news release gives more than 3,700 participants. The sources do not explain the difference, so the write-up does not use a single headcount. Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) is stepping up security and fare enforcement at several light rail stations as part of a new 90-day initiative launching Monday, November 16. Called Operation Access , the program will bring a more visible uniformed presence to key stations across the network, the agency says. Riders will see DART police officers, fare enforcement officers, and transit security officers at designated locations, according to a press release. As part of the initiative, all riders boarding at Pearl/Arts District Station and West End Station will pass through barriers and undergo mandatory fare validation before boarding. Those stations may experience brief delays during peak travel periods, although DART expects any additional wait times to be minimal, they say. In addition to the two downtown stations, uniformed enforcement teams will be stationed at Bachman, Forest Lane, LBJ/Skillman, MLK Jr., and 8th & Corinth stations. According to DART, the seven stations serve as important entry and exit points for passengers traveling to and from downtown. Placing officers and security personnel at those locations will create a more consistent presence along key rail corridors while supporting fare compliance and the agency's code of conduct. The initiative is intended to improve safety and fare compliance while helping DART better understand how passengers move through the system as it evaluates the possibility of expanding fare-gated access across the light rail network. "At its core, Operation Access is about creating the transit experience our riders deserve," says DART Chief of Police Charles Cato in the release. "When customers see a consistent security presence, know that fares are being checked, and feel confident that everyone is following the same rules, it creates a safer and more comfortable environment for everyone." Cato says the first phase will allow DART to provide those benefits immediately while gathering information to help plan for the future. DART President and CEO Nathaniel P. Ford Sr. also describes Operation Access as an important step in modernizing fare enforcement. Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) is stepping up security and fare enforcement at several light rail stations as part of a new 90-day initiative launching Monday, November 16. Called Operation Access , the program will bring a more visible uniformed presence to key stations across the network, the agency says. Riders will see DART police officers, fare enforcement officers, and transit security officers at designated locations, according to a press release. As part of the initiative, all riders boarding at Pearl/Arts District Station and West End Station will pass through barriers and undergo mandatory fare validation before boarding. Those stations may experience brief delays during peak travel periods, although DART expects any additional wait times to be minimal, they say. In addition to the two downtown stations, uniformed enforcement teams will be stationed at Bachman, Forest Lane, LBJ/Skillman, MLK Jr., and 8th & Corinth stations. According to DART, the seven stations serve as important entry and exit points for passengers traveling to and from downtown. Placing officers and security personnel at those locations will create a more consistent presence along key rail corridors while supporting fare compliance and the agency's code of conduct. "When customers see a consistent security presence, know that fares are being checked, and feel confident that everyone is following the same rules, it creates a safer and more comfortable environment for everyone." passages: It was the resignation heard across the world.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down .
“It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said.
Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
“Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

extraction.body: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking. Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom. Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.” Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch. extraction.body: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking. Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom. Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.” Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch. She is based in New York City. You can contact or verify outreach from Dominic by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at +1 646 831-7565 on Signal. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. "If that direction changes, it'll be a big blow to so many young companies," said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang's absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. "Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud," Dawn Capital's Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang's eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren't hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia's investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang's rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. "She's much more conservative," one investor said of Kress. "I don't think she's going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going." Nvidia's biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. "Jensen's initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that," Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe's rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . "Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe," Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe "would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill." It's also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang's Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia's investment crown, "depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem," he said. CUDA is Nvidia's software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker's participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. "When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe," Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking. Even so, few believe that Nvidia's investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom. Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that "founders and leaders must be held accountable," and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. "That talent will, and must, continue to thrive."

However, if the most optimistic forecasts for 2030 hold true, you might need less than one Bitcoin to become a millionaire. So how much Bitcoin do you need to be a millionaire by 2030? Bitcoin trades 49% below its $126,080 all-time high from October 2025 and has dropped 20.8% in the past month after reaching a 30-day high of $84,082. Even so, long-term predictions still point to six- and seven-figure prices. ARK Invest expects around $761,000 per coin by 2030, while Strategy executive chairman Michael Saylor believes Bitcoin could hit $1 million before the decade ends, as a look at whether Bitcoin can reach $1 million showed. At $64,664, $1 million buys about 15.5 Bitcoins. That's the number you would need if Bitcoin's price doesn't rise from here, and the same math applies to $1,000 in Bitcoin over five years. Bitcoin's market cap, its price multiplied by the coins in circulation, stands at about $1.30 trillion, with around 20.11 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million. Since the circulating supply keeps increasing, the market needs more money to reach previous price levels than it did in earlier cycles. For instance, on November 8, 2021, Bitcoin closed at $67,539 with a market cap of $1.28 trillion. Although the price is lower now, the market cap is higher because miners have added new coins, meaning future targets will require more capital than they did in past cycles. If Bitcoin recovers to its all-time high of $126,080—95% above its current price—you would need only about 7.9 Bitcoins to reach $1 million. At $64,664, buying that amount would cost roughly $513,000. This scenario is optimistic but plausible, since Bitcoin has traded at that price before. However, the trend points the other way for now. Bitcoin is trading below its 50-day moving average of $80,159 (24% above) and its 200-day average of $72,982 (13% above). When prices stay below both of these averages, sellers typically dominate the market. ETF activity reflects the same trend. Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, have seen net outflows for seven consecutive sessions—from November 5 to November 13—according to SoSoValue. Their cumulative net inflows have dropped from $58 billion on October 21 to $54.6 billion. ARK Invest has the most detailed 2030 Bitcoin forecast among the asset managers 24/7 Wall St. has covered. Its model assumes about 2.5% of the roughly $200 trillion managed by global fund managers flows into Bitcoin and projects a $16 trillion market cap, or about $761,000 per coin, within a range of $300,000 to $1.5 million. The smaller Bitcoin amounts require substantial price increases, with ARK's base scenario needing a jump to a $16 trillion market cap from $1.30 trillion now. These forecasts were made before Bitcoin's peak in October 2025, and as of August 2026, ARK had not adjusted them. Bernstein believes Bitcoin could reach $1 million, but not until 2033, while Standard Chartered lowered its 2026 target from $150,000 to $100,000 in February. A reasonable plan aims for somewhere between 7.9 and 15.5 Bitcoins. A rebound to the all-time high seems more achievable than ARK's projection of $761,000 per coin, and the 1.3-Bitcoin requirement appears unlikely, as it would need an enormous increase in Bitcoin's market cap, a gap that a look at how much one Bitcoin could be worth in 2030 also highlights. To reach the all-time-high case, Bitcoin first needs to recover its 50-day average of about $80,159. Next, cumulative ETF inflows should rise above $58 billion again, followed by a break past $126,080. The next halving, which will cut the reward paid to miners, is expected in April 2028. If Bitcoin hasn't surpassed $126,080 by then, ARK's targets may slip further out of reach, making 7.9 Bitcoins the more realistic number to plan for. Bitcoin trades 49% below its $126,080 all-time high from October 2025 and has dropped 20.8% in the past month after reaching a 30-day high of $84,082. Even so, long-term predictions still point to six- and seven-figure prices. ARK Invest expects around $761,000 per coin by 2030, while Strategy executive chairman Michael Saylor believes Bitcoin could hit $1 million before the decade ends, as a look at whether Bitcoin can reach $1 million showed. At $64,664, $1 million buys about 15.5 Bitcoins. That’s the number you would need if Bitcoin’s price doesn’t rise from here, and the same mat h applies to $1,000 in Bitcoin over five years . Bitcoin’s market cap, its price multiplied by the coins in circulation, stands at about $1.30 trillion, with around 20.11 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million. Since the circulating supply keeps increasing, the market needs more money to reach previous price levels than it did in earlier cycles. For instance, on November 8, 2021, Bitcoin closed at $67,539 with a market cap of $1.28 trillion. Although the price is lower now, the market cap is higher because miners have added new coins, meaning future targets will require more capital than they did in past cycles. If Bitcoin recovers to its all-time high of $126,080—95% above its current price—you would need only about 7.9 Bitcoins to reach $1 million. At $64,664, buying that amount would cost roughly $513,000. This scenario is optimistic but plausible, since Bitcoin has traded at that price before. However, the trend points the other way for now. Bitcoin is trading below its 50-day moving average of $80,159 (24% above) and its 200-day average of $72,982 (13% above). When prices stay below both of these averages, sellers typically dominate the market. ETF activity reflects the same trend. Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, have seen net outflows for seven consecutive sessions—from November 5 to November 13—according to SoSoValue. Their cumulative net inflows have dropped from $58 billion on October 21 to $54.6 billion. ARK Invest has the most detailed 2030 Bitcoin forecast among the asset managers 24/7 Wall St. has covered. Its model assumes about 2.5% of the roughly $200 trillion managed by global fund managers flows into Bitcoin and projects a $16 trillion market cap, or about $761,000 per coin, within a range of $300,000 to $1.5 million. The smaller Bitcoin amounts require substantial price increases, with ARK’s base scenario needing a jump to a $16 trillion market cap from $1.30 trillion now. These forecasts were made before Bitcoin’s peak in October 2025, and as of August 2026, ARK had not adjusted them. Bernstein believes Bitcoin could reach $1 million, but not until 2033, while Standard Chartered lowered its 2026 target from $150,000 to $100,000 in February. A reasonable plan aims for somewhere between 7.9 and 15.5 Bitcoins. However, if the most optimistic forecasts for 2030 hold true, you might need less than one Bitcoin to become a millionaire.
So how much Bitcoin do you need to be a millionaire by 2030?
A reasonable plan aims for somewhere between 7.9 and 15.5 Bitcoins.

A rebound to the all-time high seems more achievable than ARK's projection of $761,000 per coin, and the 1.3-Bitcoin requirement appears unlikely, as it would need an enormous increase in Bitcoin's market cap, a gap that a look at how much one Bitcoin could be worth in 2030 also highlights.
Even so, long-term predictions still point to six- and seven-figure prices.

Its model assumes about 2.5% of the roughly $200 trillion managed by global fund managers flows into Bitcoin and projects a $16 trillion market cap, or about $761,000 per coin, within a range of $300,000 to $1.5 million.
His work focuses on price levels, spot ETF flows, on-chain data and the regulatory decisions that move crypto markets, written so a first-time buyer and a seasoned trader can both use it.
Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.

A reasonable plan aims for somewhere between 7.9 and 15.5 Bitcoins.
Bitcoin trades 49% below its $126,080 all-time high from October 2025 and has dropped 20.8% in the past month after reaching a 30-day high of $84,082.
Even so, long-term predictions still point to six- and seven-figure prices.
Bitcoin sits far below its record high, and doubling your money by 2030 would demand a market value few assets have ever reached.
Four forces, from ETF outflows to a looming halving, will decide…
Which hurdles stand between the king of crypto and a 2030 moonshot,…
Weakening ETF demand, a 2028 halving, and a stalled Senate bill will decide which targets survive, and one popular dream may…
That’s the number you would need if Bitcoin’s price doesn’t rise from here, and the same mat h applies to $1,000 in Bitcoin over five years .
This scenario is optimistic but plausible, since Bitcoin has traded at that price before.
Bitcoin is trading below its 50-day moving average of $80,159 (24% above) and its 200-day average of $72,982 (13% above).
Bitcoin and Solana just suffered brutal weekly losses, and Wall Street's boldest forecasts now look a long way off.

Bitcoin’s market cap, its price multiplied by the coins in circulation, stands at about $1.30 trillion, with around 20.11 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million. Since the circulating supply keeps increasing, the market needs more money to reach previous price levels than it did in earlier cycles.

For instance, on November 8, 2021, Bitcoin closed at $67,539 with a market cap of $1.28 trillion. Although the price is lower now, the market cap is higher because miners have added new coins, meaning future targets will require more capital than they did in past cycles.

If Bitcoin recovers to its all-time high of $126,080—95% above its current price—you would need only about 7.9 Bitcoins to reach $1 million. At $64,664, buying that amount would cost roughly $513,000.

This scenario is optimistic but plausible, since Bitcoin has traded at that price before. However, the trend points the other way for now. Bitcoin is trading below its 50-day moving average of $80,159 (24% above) and its 200-day average of $72,982 (13% above). When prices stay below both of these averages, sellers typically dominate the market.

ETF activity reflects the same trend. Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, have seen net outflows for seven consecutive sessions—from November 5 to November 13—according to SoSoValue. Their cumulative net inflows have dropped from $58 billion on October 21 to $54.6 billion.

ARK Invest has the most detailed 2030 Bitcoin forecast among the asset managers 24/7 Wall St. has covered. Its model assumes about 2.5% of the roughly $200 trillion managed by global fund managers flows into Bitcoin and projects a $16 trillion market cap, or about $761,000 per coin, within a range of $300,000 to $1.5 million.

The smaller Bitcoin amounts require substantial price increases, with ARK’s base scenario needing a jump to a $16 trillion market cap from $1.30 trillion now. These forecasts were made before Bitcoin’s peak in October 2025, and as of August 2026, ARK had not adjusted them. Bernstein believes Bitcoin could reach $1 million, but not until 2033, while Standard Chartered lowered its 2026 target from $150,000 to $100,000 in February.

A reasonable plan aims for somewhere between 7.9 and 15.5 Bitcoins. A rebound to the all-time high seems more achievable than ARK’s projection of $761,000 per coin, and the 1.3-Bitcoin requirement appears unlikely, as it would need an enormous increase in Bitcoin’s market cap, a gap that a look at how much one Bitcoin could be worth in 2030 also highlights.

To reach the all-time-high case, Bitcoin first needs to recover its 50-day average of about $80,159. Next, cumulative ETF inflows should rise above $58 billion again, followed by a break past $126,080. The next halving, which will cut the reward paid to miners, is expected in April 2028. If Bitcoin hasn’t surpassed $126,080 by then, ARK’s targets may slip further out of reach, making 7.9 Bitcoins the more realistic number to plan for.
